Must retrieve the specific performance results (e.g., precision/recall/F1 or accuracy) reported on the CoNLL-2008 in-domain test set that are attributed to Johansson and Nugues (2008), from the relevant table or text passage.

Must correctly associate the retrieved CoNLL-2008 in-domain test set results with the Johansson and Nugues (2008) system or model as described in the paper, not with other baselines or the authors’ own model.

Must explicitly state that the retrieved Johansson and Nugues (2008) performance numbers correspond to the CoNLL-2008 in-domain test set, distinguishing them from any out-of-domain or other dataset results mentioned elsewhere in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize the evaluation of syntactic contribution to SRL, including which parsers are used by prior syntax-aware SRL models and what metric is proposed?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper proposes to quantitatively evaluate the syntactic contribution to SRL using the ratio of Sem-F1 to LAS (Sem-F1 / LAS) as an evaluation measure.
Must define Sem-F1 explicitly as the labeled F1 score for semantic dependencies, matching the terminology used in the paper.
Must define LAS explicitly as the labeled attachment score for syntactic dependencies, matching the terminology used in the paper.

Must identify that different syntax-aware SRL models use different syntactic parsers, specifically that PathLSTM SRL (Roth and Lapata, 2016) uses mate-tools and GCN-based SRL (Marcheggiani and Titov, 2017) uses the BIST parser.
Must retrieve the reference to Surdeanu et al., CoNLL-2008 Shared Task as the source or precedent for the evaluation setup or metrics used for assessing syntactic and semantic dependencies.

decisions: How does the paper compare SRL performance and LAS across different models to compute the Sem-F1/LAS ratio on the CoNLL-2009 English test set?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison concerns the Sem-F1/LAS ratio, defined as semantic F1 score divided by labeled attachment score (LAS), on the CoNLL-2009 English test set.
Must retrieve from the relevant results table the three metrics columns explicitly labeled (or clearly corresponding to) 'LAS', 'Sem-F1', and 'Sem-F1/LAS' for the compared models.
Must extract the row corresponding to the baseline model 'Marcheggiani and Titov, 2017' from the results table that reports LAS and Sem-F1 on CoNLL-2009 English.

Must extract the rows for the three variants of the authors' model labeled (or equivalently described as) 'Ours + CoNLL-2009 predicted', 'Ours + Auto syntax', and 'Ours + Gold syntax' from the same results table.
Must locate and use the specific experimental results section (or subsection) that reports SRL performance on the CoNLL-2009 English test set, rather than results from other datasets or languages.

decisions: How does the paper generate syntactic inputs of varying quality for experiments on the impact of syntax in semantic role labeling?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a procedure to obtain syntactic input of different quality levels by deliberately corrupting or perturbing parse trees.
Must explain that the method produces random errors in the output syntactic parse tree rather than using only gold or off-the-shelf parses.
Must specify that the corruption process is controlled by an input error probability distribution that determines how likely each syntactic element is to be modified.
Must describe that the concrete modification operation consists of changing or reassigning the syntactic heads of nodes in the dependency tree.

Must identify and draw from the section that details the faulty or noisy syntactic tree generator (e.g., the experimental setup or data preparation subsection describing syntactic noise injection), not from unrelated parts such as model architecture or evaluation metrics.

decisions: How does syntactic parsing quality (LAS) affect the semantic F1 performance of 1st-order vs 10th-order SRL models on the CoNLL-2009 English test set when using syntactic inputs generated from STG?

requirements.description: Must identify that the syntactic inputs used in the analysis are generated from an STG (syntactic) parser or model, explicitly referencing STG as the source of syntax.
Must distinguish between 1st-order and 10th-order SRL models as different k-order variants of the proposed argument labeling/pruning approach, explicitly naming both '1st-order' and '10th-order' SRL.

Must state that the 10th-order SRL model exhibits relatively stable semantic F1 performance across different levels of syntactic quality (e.g., varying LAS), i.e., its performance is largely insensitive to syntax quality changes.

Must state that the 1st-order SRL model shows overall better semantic role labeling performance than the 10th-order model when varying syntactic quality, explicitly indicating that the 1st-order model yields higher scores overall.

Must indicate that the comparison of 1st-order and 10th-order SRL models with respect to syntactic quality (LAS vs semantic F1) is conducted on the CoNLL-2009 English test set, explicitly naming this dataset/split.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions about the role of syntax in dependency SRL and the proposed future work directions?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper presents an effective model for dependency SRL that uses an extended k-order argument pruning (or k-order pruning) mechanism, explicitly linking the model to dependency SRL.

Must report that the performance gap between syntax-enhanced and syntax-agnostic SRL models has been significantly reduced, explicitly mentioning a reduction from a previously larger gap (e.g., 'from as high as X') to a smaller remaining performance loss.
Must explicitly conclude that high-quality syntactic parses (or high-quality syntax) improve or enhance SRL performance, reflecting the paper’s final takeaway about syntax utility.
Must extract from the paper’s conclusion or future work section the stated goal to develop a more effective syntax-agnostic SRL system as a future research direction.
Must extract from the paper’s conclusion or future work section the stated plan to explore or design syntactic integration methods based on high-quality syntax as a future research direction.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper’s efficient low-rank multimodal fusion framework supports multimodal sentiment and emotion analysis, including cross-modal interactions, multimodal representations, and computational efficiency?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper addresses multimodal fusion for sentiment and/or emotion analysis, explicitly linking the fusion method to analyzing speakers' behaviors or utterances (e.g., sentiment intensity of phrases like "This movie is sick").

Must describe that the proposed approach uses low-rank multimodal fusion with modality-specific factors to model cross-modal interactions between at least two modalities (e.g., language and speaker behavior).

Must explain that the method produces a joint multimodal representation by integrating multiple unimodal representations into a single compact representation, using terminology equivalent to "multimodal representation."

Must explicitly mention that the proposed low-rank fusion method improves or targets computational efficiency compared to prior tensor-based multimodal fusion approaches, referring to reduced dimensionality or complexity.

Must reference the part of the paper (e.g., experiments, applications, or task description) where multimodal sentiment or emotion analysis is used as the primary evaluation or application task for the proposed fusion method.

decisions: Does the slide correctly present the example utterance and the prior Tensor Fusion Network baseline in the context of computational efficiency for multimodal sentiment analysis?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper addresses computational efficiency issues of tensor-based multimodal fusion methods (e.g., Tensor Fusion Network) due to exponential growth in tensor dimensionality and complexity.
Must explicitly recognize Tensor Fusion Network (TFN) as a prior tensor-based multimodal fusion approach that the proposed low-rank multimodal fusion method is compared against or improves upon.
Must retrieve the full citation information for Tensor Fusion Network for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis, including that it is by Zadeh et al. and published in 2017.
Must extract from the related work or background section the description that TFN uses tensor representations for multimodal sentiment analysis, establishing it as a baseline for the current work.

Must identify that the example sentence "This movie is sick" is used in the paper as an illustrative multimodal sentiment analysis utterance (e.g., demonstrating how multimodal fusion is applied to sentiment classification).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s transition from full tensor-based multimodal fusion to an efficient low-rank fusion approach, including the role of tensor decomposition and Language Tensor Fusion Networks?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper moves from full tensor-based multimodal fusion representations to a low-rank fusion formulation, explicitly mentioning the reduction of exponential dimensionality or computational complexity.
Must describe that the proposed method rearranges the computation of the multimodal fusion operation so that it does not explicitly construct the full high-order input tensor.
Must explain that the approach uses a decomposition of the input tensor (e.g., low-rank or factorized tensor decomposition) into modality-specific factors to achieve efficient fusion.

Must reference and correctly characterize the part of the paper that introduces or formalizes Language Tensor Fusion Networks as a prior tensor-based multimodal fusion method (e.g., in the background or related work section).

Must explicitly connect Language Tensor Fusion Networks to the motivation for low-rank multimodal fusion, indicating that the proposed method is an efficient alternative or extension to such tensor fusion networks.

decisions: What definition of tensor rank, in the context of Canonical Polyadic (CP) decomposition, does the paper provide that is needed to generate this slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the rank of a tensor is defined as the minimum number of rank-1 components (or vector tuples) whose sum exactly reconstructs the tensor.
Must describe that in CP decomposition a rank-1 tensor is formed as the outer product of modality-specific vectors (one vector per mode of the tensor).

Must extract the definition of tensor rank from the part of the paper where CP (Canonical Polyadic) or CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition is formally introduced (e.g., preliminaries or background section on tensor algebra).

Must reference any figure or equation in the paper that explicitly illustrates a tensor being written as a sum of rank-1 outer products (e.g., an equation showing X = sum_{r=1}^R a_r ∘ b_r ∘ c_r) and connect this to the definition of rank as the number R of such terms.

Must explicitly link the phrase 'minimum number' in the definition to the fact that no smaller number of rank-1 terms can exactly reconstruct the tensor, distinguishing this from an arbitrary decomposition with more terms.

decisions: How does the paper describe handling the dimensionality of the multimodal representation when performing modality-specific decomposition in its low-rank multimodal fusion framework?

requirements.description: Must state that during modality-specific decomposition, the dimensionality of the resulting multimodal representation is explicitly retained (i.e., not expanded or reduced).

Must describe the modality-specific decomposition step as part of the proposed low-rank multimodal fusion method, indicating that decomposition is applied separately to each modality or modality-specific factor.
Must explain that the decomposition is designed to avoid the exponential increase in tensor dimensionality that occurs in prior tensor-based multimodal fusion methods.

Must reference the part of the paper where the authors formally define or describe the modality-specific factorization/decomposition used in their low-rank multimodal fusion model (e.g., the model or method description section).
Must connect the retention of multimodal representation dimension during decomposition to the goal of making the fusion more efficient in terms of computational complexity or parameter count.

decisions: Which datasets and their key annotation properties are used for sentiment analysis, speaker trait recognition, and emotion recognition in this paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that three distinct tasks are covered: Sentiment Analysis, Speaker Trait Recognition, and Emotion Recognition, and present them as separate dataset/task categories.
Must state that the sentiment analysis data comes from 93 movie reviews, matching the exact count '93' and the source type 'movie reviews'.
Must report that the speaker trait recognition dataset consists of 1000 full video clips and includes 16 types of speaker traits, matching both the number '1000' and '16'.

Must specify the annotation granularity for each task: segment-level annotations for sentiment analysis, video-level annotations for speaker trait recognition, and segment-level annotations for emotion recognition.
Must state that the emotion recognition dataset has 10 classes of emotions, matching the exact number '10'.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the evaluation metrics and sub-metrics used to compare low-rank multimodal fusion against full-rank tensor fusion in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the comparison is specifically between the proposed low-rank multimodal fusion method and a full-rank tensor fusion baseline (or equivalent full tensor fusion model), as indicated in the experimental comparison section.

Must retrieve from the relevant results table the use of 'MAE' and 'Correlation' as evaluation metrics for at least one regression-style task (e.g., sentiment intensity or similar), matching the slide headers 'MAE' and 'Correlation'.

Must retrieve from the same or related results table the classification metrics 'Acc-2', 'F1', and 'Acc-7' as distinct evaluation metrics, corresponding to binary accuracy, F1, and 7-class accuracy used in the paper.
Must identify and extract the emotion-specific F1 metrics 'F1-Happy' and 'F1-Sad' from the appropriate experimental results table where per-emotion F1 scores are reported.

Must base all retrieved metric names (MAE, Correlation, Acc-2, F1, Acc-7, F1-Happy, F1-Sad) on the paper's experimental results section (e.g., tables comparing models), not from the abstract or introduction.

decisions: What information from the paper is needed to present the comparison of Mean Average Error (MAE) for the Deep Fusion (Nojavanasghari et al., 2016) baseline in the 'Compare with State of the Art Approaches' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison is based on the Mean Average Error (MAE) metric, explicitly using the term 'Mean Average Error (MAE)'.
Must retrieve the MAE value(s) reported in the paper for the Deep Fusion baseline method and associate them with that method in the comparison context (e.g., from a results table comparing methods).
Must recognize 'Deep Fusion' as an external baseline method (not the proposed method) used for state-of-the-art comparison, as cited in the paper's experimental or comparison section.

Must extract information from the section where state-of-the-art or baseline methods are quantitatively compared (e.g., an 'Experiments', 'Results', or 'Comparison with State of the Art' section) rather than from unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.
Must correctly associate the citation 'Nojavanasghari et al., 2016' with the Deep Fusion method as it appears in the paper (e.g., in a results table caption, legend, or baseline description).

decisions: How does the proposed low-rank multimodal fusion method quantitatively compare against the top 2 state-of-the-art approaches in terms of MAE, Correlation, F1-Angry, and F1-Sad?

requirements.description: Must retrieve from the comparison table the MAE values for the proposed method and each of the top 2 state-of-the-art baselines for at least one evaluation setting explicitly labeled with 'MAE'.

Must retrieve from the comparison table the Correlation values for the proposed method and each of the top 2 state-of-the-art baselines for at least one evaluation setting explicitly labeled with 'Correlation'.

Must retrieve from the comparison table the F1 scores for the 'Angry' emotion class (explicitly labeled 'F1-Angry' or equivalent) for the proposed method and each of the top 2 state-of-the-art baselines.
Must retrieve from the comparison table the F1 scores for the 'Sad' emotion class (explicitly labeled 'F1-Sad' or equivalent) for the proposed method and each of the top 2 state-of-the-art baselines.

Must identify the specific figure or table (e.g., 'Table X: Comparison with state-of-the-art methods') that jointly reports MAE, Correlation, F1-Angry, and F1-Sad for the proposed method and at least two baseline methods.

decisions: How does the paper define and report its efficiency metric for training and testing, in terms of data samples processed per second?

requirements.description: Must state that the efficiency metric used in the paper is explicitly defined as the number of data samples processed per second.

Must retrieve from the relevant experiment section, table, or figure the efficiency values reported separately for training and for testing (i.e., two distinct numbers or ranges in samples per second).

Must identify and use the specific section or subsection where computational efficiency or runtime performance is discussed (e.g., an 'Efficiency', 'Runtime', or 'Complexity' analysis section) as the source for the metric definition and values.

Must correctly interpret any figure or table that reports throughput or runtime (e.g., a plot or table with units in samples/s) and extract from it the training and testing efficiency values, if they are presented visually rather than in text.

Must note the experimental setting under which the efficiency metric is measured (e.g., hardware setup or batch size) if this context is specified alongside the samples-per-second values in the paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stated overall objective for participating in WAT 2015?

requirements.description: Must state that the main goal is to test or evaluate several extremely simple translation techniques or approaches, not to introduce a complex new model.
Must indicate that these simple techniques are explicitly described as having been reported as efficient or effective in previous research or prior work.
Must extract the paper’s motivation or objective statement (e.g., from the introduction or task description) that links the use of WAT 2015 to evaluating these simple techniques.
Must capture the conditional intention that if the simple techniques are shown to work (i.e., perform well in evaluation), then they should be used more widely or more broadly adopted.
Must connect the objective of testing simple techniques specifically to the WAT 2015 evaluation setting, including the use of WAT’s human evaluation as a key reason for conducting the tests.

decisions: What specific translation approaches and directions did the NICT team report as key outcomes in their WAT 2015 systems?

requirements.description: Must state that a reverse pre-reordering approach was applied specifically to the Japanese-to-English (JE) translation task.
Must state that a character-based approach was used specifically for the Korean-to-Japanese (KJ) translation task.
Must identify reverse pre-reordering as a pre-reordering method applied before phrase-based SMT for Japanese-to-English translation, as described in the abstract.
Must identify that the Korean-to-Japanese translation processing was conducted purely on the character level, not word level, as described in the abstract.
Must extract both JE and KJ task descriptions from the same summary context (e.g., abstract or system description section) to jointly present them as overall results or key approaches.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and contrast the definitions, limitations, and roles of extractive versus abstractive summarization as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that extractive summarization is defined in the paper as selecting parts (typically sentences) directly from the original text to form a summary.
Must state that abstractive summarization is defined in the paper as generating novel sentences using natural language generation techniques, rather than only copying source text.
Must state that the paper characterizes extractive summarization as too restrictive because it does not allow paraphrasing of the original text.
Must report that the paper notes most past work in summarization has been extractive, in contrast to the abstractive approach it studies.
Must state that the paper presents abstractive summarization as more flexible and human-like, and as necessary for future progress in summarization research.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve the specific CNN/Daily Mail article content used as the example input for the pointer-generator summarization model, as reflected in the 'Cnn Daily Mail dataset' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide text is drawn from a CNN/Daily Mail news article example used in the paper to illustrate the summarization task on the CNN/Daily Mail dataset (not from the model description or other datasets).

Must retrieve the specific article snippet mentioning 'The papal bill Pope Francis insisted on paying himself... before catching the bus home after winning the election' as it appears in the paper's CNN/Daily Mail example.
Must retrieve the sentence fragment about transportation choice, including the phrase 'also chose to use a bus instead of a chauffeur driven car' from the CNN/Daily Mail example text in the paper.

Must retrieve the detail about Pope Francis's personal style, including the phrase '+ The 76-year-old has eschewed ceremonial traditions for a more humble approach' from the example article text in the paper.

Must locate and use the section or subsection where the paper presents concrete CNN/Daily Mail article examples (input documents) for the summarization model, rather than synthetic or Wikipedia examples.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and describe the example illustrating the basic sequence-to-sequence attention model used for summarization in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example on the slide illustrates a standard sequence-to-sequence attentional model (without the pointer-generator extension), as described in the model background of the paper.

Must reproduce the exact example sentence pair used in the paper’s illustration of the sequence-to-sequence attention model: the source text "Germany emerge victorious in win against Argentina on Saturday" and the partial summary "Germany beat Argentina" (including the <START> and STOP tokens as shown).

Must explain that the example demonstrates how the decoder generates the target summary token-by-token starting from the <START> token and ending at the STOP token, consistent with the paper’s description of the baseline attentional seq2seq summarization process.

Must draw from the section of the paper that introduces or reviews the baseline sequence-to-sequence attentional summarization model (prior to introducing the pointer-generator mechanism), rather than from sections describing the hybrid pointer-generator or coverage mechanisms.

Must state that in this baseline example the model is performing abstractive summarization by generating a shorter paraphrased summary ("Germany beat Argentina") from the longer source sentence, as described in the paper’s explanation of abstractive seq2seq summarization.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify the two main problems of standard abstractive seq2seq summarization and the corresponding high-level solutions proposed in the pointer-generator network paper?

requirements.description: Must state that one identified problem with standard neural abstractive summarization is inaccurate reproduction of factual details (e.g., wrong entities or outcomes such as who beat whom).
Must state that a second identified problem with standard neural abstractive summarization is repetition, i.e., the model generating the same phrase or clause multiple times in a row.
Must describe the proposed solution to the factual inaccuracy problem as a hybrid pointer-generator mechanism that can copy words directly from the source text via a pointer.

Must describe the proposed solution to the repetition problem as a mechanism that penalizes repeatedly attending to the same parts of the source text (i.e., a coverage or attention-penalty mechanism).

Must attribute both problems and both corresponding solutions to the paper's early problem-motivation or model-introduction discussion (e.g., the introductory description of shortcomings and the high-level overview of the proposed architecture), not to experimental or related-work sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify that the paper’s model combines extractive copying with abstractive generation in a sequence-to-sequence framework, and situate it relative to prior copying/compression work?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed model combines both extractive (copying from the source text) and abstractive (generating novel words) summarization within a single sequence-to-sequence architecture, i.e., a 'best of both worlds' approach.
Must explicitly describe the use of a copying or pointer mechanism that allows the decoder to directly copy words from the source text, as opposed to only generating from a fixed vocabulary.
Must distinguish between 'Source Text' (input article) and 'Target' (summary) in the model’s formulation, indicating that the model learns to map from source text to a shorter target summary.
Must reference that the model is built on a sequence-to-sequence learning framework with attention, augmented by the pointer/copying mechanism.

Must identify and mention at least two prior works on copying/compression mechanisms that the paper cites as related work, specifically Gu et al. (2016) on incorporating copying mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence learning and Miao and Blunsom (2016) on discrete generative models for sentence compression.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and explain how the pointer-generator network copies words from the source text when generating a summary (as illustrated by the Germany–Argentina example)?

requirements.description: Must state that the pointer-generator network is a hybrid model that can both generate words from a fixed vocabulary and copy words directly from the source text via a pointing mechanism.

Must describe the role of the pointer (copy) mechanism in ensuring that specific factual tokens (e.g., named entities like 'Germany' and 'Argentina') are copied from the source text rather than freely generated.
Must cover the part of the paper where the pointer-generator architecture is formally introduced and defined, including how it modifies the standard sequence-to-sequence attentional model.

Must reference and describe the example in the paper that demonstrates copying behavior on a news-style sentence (e.g., a headline-like source text where the model copies country names or entities into the summary), analogous to the 'Germany emerge victorious in win against Argentina on Saturday' example.

Must explain that the pointer-generator network is proposed to address factual inaccuracy and repetition problems of standard abstractive sequence-to-sequence summarization models, as stated in the abstract and model motivation sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the paper’s improvements in reducing UNK tokens and repetition in generated summaries, as illustrated by the example outputs shown in the Improvements slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a pointer-generator network specifically to reduce UNK tokens in abstractive summarization outputs by enabling direct copying of words from the source text.
Must state that the paper introduces a coverage mechanism (or an equivalent explicit anti-repetition component) to reduce repeated phrases in generated summaries.

Must reference the qualitative example in the paper that contrasts a baseline seq2seq model output containing repeated phrases like 'the rio olympic games the rio olympic games' with an improved output from the proposed model that reduces such repetition.

Must reference the qualitative example in the paper that contrasts a baseline output containing UNK tokens such as 'UNK UNK was expelled from the dubai open chess tournament' with an improved output from the pointer-generator model that correctly copies the name 'gaioz nigalidze' from the source.
Must explicitly connect these qualitative examples (UNK replacement and repetition reduction) to the claimed improvements of the proposed model over the standard attentional seq2seq baseline.

decisions: How does the paper use coverage to reduce repetition in generated summaries, and what empirical effect does this have relative to human summaries?

requirements.description: Must state that coverage is defined as cumulative attention over the source sequence, explicitly equating it with "what has been covered so far" in the input.

Must identify and use the part of the paper that discusses coverage in the context of prior work on neural machine translation, explicitly referencing Tu et al. (2016), Mi et al. (2016), and Chen et al. (2016) as coverage-related or distraction-based models.

Must describe that the coverage vector is used as an additional input to the attention mechanism (i.e., attention depends not only on the current decoder state and encoder states but also on the accumulated coverage).

Must explain that the model penalizes attending to source positions that have already been heavily covered, typically via a coverage-based penalty or loss term that discourages repeatedly attending to the same locations.

Must report that the introduction of coverage reduces the repetition rate in generated summaries to a level comparable or similar to human-written summaries, as stated in the experimental results section.

decisions: How does the paper quantitatively evaluate its summarization models using ROUGE, and how do these results compare to prior abstractive baselines and Paulus et al. (2017) variants?

requirements.description: Must correctly define ROUGE as the evaluation metric used in the paper, including that it compares machine-generated summaries to human-written reference summaries and counts co-occurrence of 1-grams, 2-grams, and longest common subsequence.
Must identify from the results section or tables that Nallapati et al. 2016 is reported as the previous best abstractive summarization result used as a baseline for ROUGE comparison.

Must distinguish between the two main proposed models in the paper's experiments: (1) the pointer-generator model and (2) the pointer-generator model with coverage, as separate systems whose ROUGE scores are reported.

Must retrieve that the paper reports ROUGE results for Paulus et al. 2017's hybrid RL approach and RL-only approach, and that these are explicitly compared against the pointer-generator models in the same results table or section.

Must capture the directional qualitative comparison stated in the paper that Paulus et al. 2017's hybrid RL approach has worse ROUGE but better human evaluation than the pointer-generator models, while the RL-only approach has better ROUGE but worse human evaluation.

decisions: How does the paper characterize the limitations of ROUGE-based evaluation for news summarization, particularly in relation to lead-3 baselines and the multiplicity of valid summaries?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper explicitly notes there are many different correct ways to summarize a document, highlighting the multiplicity of valid summaries.
Must explain that ROUGE is described in the paper as relying on a strict n-gram overlap comparison to a single (or fixed) reference summary, rather than allowing for multiple valid summaries.

Must retrieve the paper's claim that using the first three sentences of a news article as a summary (the 'lead-3' baseline) achieves ROUGE scores higher than or comparable to almost any published abstractive summarization system reported in the paper.
Must identify that the 'first 3 sentences' (lead-3) baseline is used in the paper as a simple evaluation baseline for news summarization performance under ROUGE.

Must mention the paper's explanation that the strong performance of the lead-3 baseline under ROUGE is attributed at least partially to the typical structure of news articles (e.g., key information concentrated at the beginning).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the example news article lead used in the paper to illustrate that first sentences are not always good summaries, including the marked irrelevant sentence and the pointer location where the system starts?

requirements.description: Must identify that this slide illustrates the paper's core claim that the first sentence (or lead) of a news article is not always a good summary, and that the example is used to motivate the need for better summarization methods.

Must retrieve the specific example article text from the section where the authors discuss lead-based baselines or first-sentence heuristics (e.g., the introductory or motivation section that presents the Mitsukoshi Department Store robot greeter article).

Must capture the slide or figure in the paper that shows the full news lead about the Tokyo Mitsukoshi Department Store robot greeter, including the sentence explicitly labeled as 'Irrelevant' within that visual example.

Must include the visual annotation or marker in the paper (e.g., an arrow, bracket, or text label) indicating 'Our system starts here' at the specific sentence boundary within the example article, and correctly associate it with the corresponding sentence in the text.

Must distinguish between sentences in the example that are considered part of a naive lead-based summary and those highlighted by the authors as irrelevant or suboptimal, reflecting the paper's argument against simple lead baselines.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the three key structural properties that TUPA is the first parser to jointly support for UCCA (and related semantic schemes)?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed parser (TUPA) is presented as the first parser to support the *combination* of three formal properties in a single system, not just any one property individually.

Must identify "non-terminal nodes" as one of the three key properties and explain that these correspond to complex semantic units such as entities and events spanning text segments (e.g., a multi-word unit like "take a long bath").

Must identify "reentrancy" as one of the three key properties and explicitly describe it as allowing argument sharing (i.e., nodes participating in multiple super-ordinate relations, yielding DAG structures).
Must identify "discontinuity" as one of the three key properties and explicitly describe it as allowing conceptual units that are split or non-contiguous in the surface word order.

Must state that these three properties (non-terminal nodes, reentrancy, discontinuity) are presented in the paper as jointly needed to support multiple semantic schemes, explicitly including UCCA and at least one other scheme such as AMR.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of UCCA within the broader landscape of semantic representation and annotation schemes, as reflected in the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify UCCA explicitly as a semantic representation scheme and place it alongside other semantic annotation frameworks (e.g., semantic dependencies, semantic role labeling) as part of a broader landscape of linguistic structure annotation schemes.

Must retrieve and use content from the introductory or background parts of the paper where UCCA is introduced in relation to other semantic representation schemes, rather than from sections focused solely on the transition-based parser algorithm or experimental setup.

Must capture the paper’s characterization of semantic representation schemes (including UCCA) as abstracting away from syntactic detail that does not affect meaning, using wording that clearly reflects this abstraction-from-syntax notion.

Must retrieve the bibliographic information that UCCA was introduced by Abend and Rappoport (2013) and that there is a later survey by Abend and Rappoport (2017), and correctly associate these citations with UCCA and with the broader class of semantic representation schemes, respectively.

Must recognize that the paper situates UCCA among multiple semantic representation schemes (including but not limited to semantic dependencies and semantic role labeling) and convey that UCCA is one member of this larger family, not an isolated formalism.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the key properties and practical advantages of UCCA that justify using it as the target representation in this parser paper?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA is presented as a cross-linguistically applicable semantic representation framework, explicitly attributing this property to Abend and Rappoport (2013).
Must state that UCCA is described as stable under translation, explicitly attributing this property to Sulem et al. (2015).
Must state that UCCA supports a rapid and intuitive annotation interface, explicitly attributing this claim to Abend et al. (2017).
Must state that UCCA annotation is usable by non-experts, and must mention the demo or annotation interface URL (ucca-demo.cs.huji.ac.il) if present in the source text.
Must state that UCCA facilitates semantics-based human evaluation of machine output (e.g., MT or NLP systems), capturing this as a distinct practical use case mentioned in the paper.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how UCCA graph structures are defined and represented, including terminals, non-terminals, remote edges, reentrancy, and discontinuity?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA structures are represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), explicitly using the term 'directed acyclic graph' or 'DAG' as described in the paper's definition of UCCA graphs.
Must explain that text tokens correspond to terminal nodes and that complex semantic units correspond to non-terminal nodes, matching the paper's formal description of UCCA node types.

Must describe that 'remote edges' are a special edge type used to enable reentrancy for argument sharing, using the term 'remote' and connecting it to reentrancy as defined in the UCCA formalism section.
Must state that UCCA allows discontinuous phrases or units (e.g., multi-word expressions) and explicitly connect this to the possibility of discontinuous structures in the UCCA graph.

Must reference the illustrative UCCA graph example that includes labeled units such as 'D' (adverbial) and 'F' (function) over the sentence 'You want to take a long bath', and indicate that dashed or otherwise distinguished edges in that figure represent remote edges.

decisions: Does the system correctly describe the transition-based parsing framework used in the UCCA DAG parser, including its parser state, transition set, and support for UCCA-specific structural properties?

requirements.description: Must state that the parser is transition-based and processes an input sequence of tokens (w1 … wn) incrementally to construct a graph G.
Must describe the parser state as consisting of at least a stack, a buffer, and a (partially) constructed graph.
Must list the specific transition types used by the parser, including at minimum: Shift, Reduce, NodeX, Left-EdgeX, Right-EdgeX, Left-RemoteX, Right-RemoteX, Swap, and Finish.
Must explicitly mention that the transition system is designed to support non-terminal nodes, reentrancy, and discontinuity in the resulting graph structures.
Must attribute the origin of transition-based parsing to dependency parsing work by Nivre (2004) when introducing the parsing approach.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the UCCA parsing example sequence shown in the paper for the sentence 'You want to take a long bath'?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example illustrates a UCCA parsing/derivation sequence for the sentence 'You want to take a long bath'.

Must reproduce the exact four-line sequence of configurations (or nodes on the buffer/stack) as shown in the example figure or illustration: 'You want to take a long bath', 'to A C F C', 'want You to take a long bath', 'You take a long bath', 'You a long bath', in the same order and on separate lines.
Must correctly associate the label sequence 'to A C F C' with the tokens in the sentence 'You want to take a long bath' as presented in the example (i.e., not altering token order or labels).

Must state that this example is used in the paper to demonstrate intermediate configurations of the transition-based DAG parser (e.g., successive parser states or transitions) rather than being a generic UCCA annotation only.

Must locate this example within the part of the paper that explains the transition system or parsing process (e.g., the section describing the transition-based parser or illustrative parsing examples), not from unrelated sections such as experiments or related work.

decisions: How does the paper describe the oracle-generated transition sequence for parsing the example sentence 'take a long bath' during training?

requirements.description: Must state that an oracle is used to provide the transition sequence given the correct UCCA graph for the training example.

Must identify and draw from the paper's training or learning section where oracle-generated transition sequences are described (e.g., the section that explains how gold graphs are converted to transition sequences).
Must explicitly mention that the example sentence used to illustrate the oracle transitions is 'take a long bath'.

Must list the full ordered sequence of transitions for the example, including all operation names and labels, exactly as in the paper: 'Shift, Right-EdgeA, Shift, Swap, Right-EdgeP, Reduce, Shift, Shift, NodeF, Reduce, Shift, Shift, NodeC, Reduce, Shift, Right-EdgeP, Shift, Right-EdgeF, Reduce, Shift, Swap, Right-EdgeD, Reduce, Swap, Right-EdgeA, Reduce, Reduce, Shift, Shift, Left-RemoteA, Shift, Right-EdgeC, Finish'.

Must preserve the specific transition operation names and their attached labels (e.g., 'Right-EdgeA', 'Right-EdgeP', 'NodeF', 'NodeC', 'Right-EdgeF', 'Right-EdgeD', 'Left-RemoteA', 'Right-EdgeC') without altering or omitting any label.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the TUPA model’s transition prediction approach, classifier variants, and feature set as described in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the TUPA model learns to greedily predict the next transition based on the current parser state (i.e., a greedy transition-based parsing strategy).

Must list all three classifier variants experimented with for TUPA: (1) a sparse perceptron with sparse features following Zhang and Nivre (2011), (2) an MLP with embeddings and a feedforward neural network following Chen and Manning (2014), and (3) a BiLSTM-based model with word embeddings, a deep bidirectional LSTM, and an MLP classifier.

Must describe the feature set used by the parser, including at minimum: words, POS tags, syntactic dependencies, existing edge labels from the stack and buffer, and structural features involving parents, children, and grandchildren of nodes.
Must mention that the feature representation includes ordinal or structural features such as node height and the number of parents and children for nodes in the parse structure.
Must explain that effective lookahead is encoded via the BiLSTM-based representation (i.e., using a deep bidirectional LSTM to capture context beyond the immediate stack and buffer).

decisions: How does the paper define the out-of-domain English evaluation data used in the experimental setup?

requirements.description: Must state that the described dataset is used as out-of-domain data in the experimental setup (i.e., explicitly identify it as 'out-of-domain').
Must retrieve the description of the out-of-domain dataset from the paper's Experimental Setup / Data / Evaluation section where the corpora are defined.
Must specify that the out-of-domain data is the English part of an English-French parallel corpus.
Must name the specific source text of the out-of-domain corpus as 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.'
Must report the size of the out-of-domain dataset as 506 sentences.

decisions: What baseline parsers and UCCA-specific approximations does the paper define and compare against its proposed transition-based DAG parser?

requirements.description: Must state that there are no existing native UCCA parsers and that the paper therefore uses a conversion-based approximation of UCCA structures for baselines.
Must list the two bilexical DAG parsers used as baselines, explicitly naming DAGParser (Ribeyre et al., 2014) as transition-based and TurboParser (Almeida and Martins, 2015) as graph-based.

Must list the three tree parsers used as baselines, explicitly naming MaltParser (Nivre et al., 2007) and Stack LSTM Parser (Dyer et al., 2015) as bilexical tree parsers, and uparse (Maier, 2015) as a parser that allows non-terminals and discontinuity.
Must describe the UCCA bilexical DAG approximation procedure used for baselines, including that for tree parsers remote edges are deleted to obtain a tree structure.

Must draw all baseline-related information from the paper's baselines/experimental setup section where the authors enumerate external parsers and describe the UCCA conversion/approximation used for evaluation.

decisions: How does the paper define and use bilexical graph approximation for UCCA parsing, and what specific example structure does it present?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA graphs are first converted to bilexical dependency graphs ("bilexical dependencies") as an approximation step before parsing.

Must describe the three-step pipeline: (1) convert UCCA graphs to bilexical dependencies, (2) train bilexical parsers and apply them to test sentences, and (3) reconstruct full UCCA graphs from the bilexical parses and compare them with gold-standard UCCA graphs.
Must reference the specific example sentence "After graduation Joe moved to Paris" used in the paper to illustrate bilexical graph approximation.

Must describe that the example visualization includes a multi-line labeled structure over the sentence tokens, with rows of labels such as "L H U H", "A P A P A", "A A to Paris", and "L U A R" aligned to the words in the example sentence.

Must indicate that the reconstructed UCCA graphs obtained from bilexical parsers are explicitly evaluated by comparison against gold-standard UCCA graphs (i.e., the approximation quality is quantitatively or systematically assessed).

decisions: How does the paper define and compute evaluation metrics for comparing UCCA graphs produced by the parser against gold-standard graphs?

requirements.description: Must state that evaluation is done by comparing graphs over the same sequence of tokens and matching edges by their terminal yield and label.
Must specify that labeled precision, labeled recall, and labeled F1 scores are calculated as the core evaluation metrics for the parser.
Must describe that primary and remote edges are evaluated separately, i.e., that scores are reported independently for primary edges and for remote edges.

Must reference the example comparison of two UCCA graphs over the sentence involving 'graduation Joe moved to Paris', including the alignment of labels in the schematic rows (e.g., 'L H U H L H U' and 'A P A P A S A').

Must mention that the evaluation reports separate labeled F1 (LF), labeled precision (LP), and labeled recall (LR) values for primary edges and for remote edges, using notation such as 'Primary: LF LP LR' and 'Remote: LF LP LR'.

decisions: Does the paper show that the TUPABiLSTM parser achieves the best F-scores across all evaluation metrics, including both primary and remote edges, and remains comparable on the out-of-domain test set?

requirements.description: Must state that the TUPABiLSTM model (the transition-based UCCA parser with BiLSTM features) is reported as obtaining the highest F-scores among compared systems in the paper.
Must retrieve from the results table(s) the evaluation breakdown into primary edges and remote edges, explicitly identifying that both categories are evaluated separately.

Must report that for each of the primary and remote edge categories, the metrics used are labeled precision (LP), labeled recall (LR), and labeled F1 (LF), matching the notation in the paper's results table or evaluation section.
Must identify from the results section or table that TUPABiLSTM achieves the best (highest) LF scores for both primary and remote edges compared to all baselines on the main in-domain test set.

Must extract the statement or numerical evidence from the results section indicating that TUPABiLSTM performance is comparable on the out-of-domain test set (e.g., similar LF scores or an explicit textual claim of comparability).

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main conclusions about UCCA’s required graph properties, the capabilities and performance of the TUPA parser, and the proposed future directions and applications?

requirements.description: Must state that UCCA’s semantic distinctions require a graph structure that simultaneously includes non-terminal nodes, reentrancy, and discontinuity, as described in the paper’s problem/representation description of UCCA.

Must identify TUPA as a transition-based UCCA parser and explicitly state that it is the first parser to support UCCA and any directed acyclic graph (DAG) over the text tokens, as claimed in the paper’s description of the proposed model.
Must report that TUPA outperforms strong conversion-based baselines, as stated in the experimental results or evaluation section comparing TUPA to conversion-based approaches.
Must mention the extension to additional languages by specifying that work on a German UCCA corpus is underway, as described in the paper’s conclusion or future work section.

Must list at least three future directions or applications from the conclusion/future work section, including: (1) parsing other schemes such as AMR, (2) comparing semantic representations through conversion, and (3) applications like text simplification and MT (machine translation) evaluation.

decisions: What problem regarding the required amount of labeled training data for sentiment/document classification does the paper identify, including the approximate scale needed to surpass classical methods and the context of large-scale labeled datasets?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper identifies the required amount of labeled training data as a key problem or bottleneck for supervised sentiment/document classification.
Must report the specific quantitative claim that at least about 100k (one hundred thousand) labeled training records are needed to surpass classical methods or baselines.

Must extract this labeled-data requirement from the part of the paper that motivates the problem or introduces the need for pretraining (e.g., problem statement or introduction), not from unrelated experimental or implementation details.
Must mention that the discussion of labeled data scale is framed in the context of large-scale labeled datasets for document (or sentiment) classification, not in a different task domain.

Must correctly identify and include the publication venue and date context as given in the paper metadata (56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 15-20 July 2018, Melbourne) when reproducing or summarizing the slide content.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the specific prior work cited in the paper’s 'Previous Work' context that is relevant to pretraining sentiment classifiers with unlabeled dialog data?

requirements.description: Must identify that the referenced prior method is a 'sequence autoencoder' used as a pretraining approach for downstream tasks.
Must attribute the 'sequence autoencoder' to the paper by Dai and Le (2015) as part of the paper's previous work or related work discussion.
Must retrieve the exact citation string or author-year pair 'Dai and Le 2015' from the references or related work portion of the paper when describing prior methods.
Must recognize that this prior work is presented in the context of pretraining with unlabeled data (e.g., language model or autoencoder-based pretraining) for classification tasks.

Must distinguish the cited 'sequence autoencoder (Dai and Le 2015)' as an earlier, non-conditional pretraining approach contrasted with the paper's proposed conditional encoder-decoder pretraining using tweet-reply pairs.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main contributions and data resources as presented on the 'Our Contributions' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper proposes a pretraining strategy using unlabeled dialog data (tweet–reply or utterance–response pairs) specifically for sentiment classification.
Must specify that the pretraining is done with an encoder–decoder (conditional language) model that is later used for or adapted to sentiment classifiers.
Must report that the proposed method outperforms other semi-supervised sentiment classification methods, as claimed in the contributions or experimental results section.
Must mention the use of distant supervision signals from emoji and/or emoticons in the unlabeled dialog data as part of the training or labeling strategy.

Must provide both dataset scale figures: a labeled sentiment dataset of approximately 99.5K items and a large-scale unlabeled dialog dataset of approximately 22.3M utterance–response pairs used in the case study.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s key idea that sentiment-handling capabilities are implicitly learned from emotional conversations in an unlabeled dialog (tweet-reply) dataset via a dialog model, and correctly attribute the venue and year?

requirements.description: Must state that the approach relies on using emotional conversations in an unlabeled dialog dataset (e.g., tweet-reply pairs) as the primary data source for pretraining.
Must describe that sentiment-handling capabilities are learned implicitly by training a dialog (encoder-decoder / conditional language) model, rather than by direct supervised sentiment labels.
Must explicitly connect the dialog modeling objective to sentiment classification, i.e., explain that the dialog model pretraining is used to improve a downstream sentiment classifier.

Must extract the paper’s main contribution statement or key idea description (typically in the abstract or introduction) that explains using unlabeled dialog data for pretraining sentiment classifiers.

Must correctly identify and reproduce the publication venue and date as '56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 15-20 July 2018, Melbourne' or an equivalent string containing all of: '56th', 'Association for Computational Linguistics', '2018', and 'Melbourne'.

decisions: What data resources does the proposed method use for pretraining and supervised sentiment classification in the tweet-based dialog setting?

requirements.description: Must identify that the method relies on a large-scale dialog corpus consisting of unlabeled utterance-response tweet (tweet-reply) pairs, as described in the data/pretraining setup of the paper.
Must identify that the method also uses a labeled dataset consisting of a moderate number of tweets annotated with sentiment labels, as described in the supervised training setup of the paper.

Must extract both the definition/description of the large-scale unlabeled dialog corpus and the labeled sentiment dataset from the section(s) describing datasets or experimental setup (e.g., data, corpus, or experiments section).

Must explicitly distinguish the roles of the two datasets by stating that the unlabeled utterance-response tweet pairs are used for pretraining (via the encoder-decoder conditional language model) and the labeled sentiment tweets are used for training/evaluating the sentiment classifier.

Must retrieve and preserve the characterization of dataset scale using the contrastive phrasing from the paper (i.e., that the dialog corpus is 'large-scale' or 'a large number' and the labeled sentiment dataset is 'moderate' in size or 'a moderate number').

decisions: How does the paper describe the preparation of the large-scale tweet–reply dataset used for pretraining the sentiment classifier?

requirements.description: Must state that the dataset consists of pairs of an utterance tweet and its response tweet (tweet–reply pairs).
Must report the total dataset size as 22.3 million (22.3M) tweet–reply pairs, matching the value given in the paper.
Must identify that the tweet–reply pairs are extracted from Twitter Firehose data, not from any other Twitter API or external corpus.
Must mention that the dataset is split into training, validation, and test subsets, reflecting the three-way partition shown in the data preparation description/table.
Must attribute this information to the paper's data preparation or dataset construction description (e.g., the section that explains how the 22.3M tweet–reply pairs were collected and partitioned).

decisions: How is the encoder-decoder dialog model architected in terms of embedding sizes, hidden representation, output dimensions, and parameter sharing between encoder and decoder LSTMs?

requirements.description: Must identify that the model is an encoder-decoder LSTM-RNN dialog model where both encoder RNN and decoder RNN are explicitly mentioned as separate components ("encoder RNN" and "decoder RNN").
Must state that the LSTMs of the encoder and decoder share parameters, using wording equivalent to "LSTMs of the encoder and decoder share the parameter."
Must specify the dimensionality of the embedding layer as mapping 4000 tokens to 256-dimensional embeddings ("Embedding layer: 4000 tokens, 256 elements").
Must specify that the encoder produces a 1024-dimensional representation ("Representation which encoder gives: 1024 elements").

Must describe the decoder’s output pathway including a 256-dimensional readout layer and an output layer over 4000 tokens ("Decoder's readout layer: 256 elements" and "Decoder's output layer: 4000 tokens"), and reference the token IDs xt/yt and outputs ot as shown in the model diagram.

decisions: How does the sentiment classification model architecture relate to the dialog model, and how does it output sentiment predictions?

requirements.description: Must state that the encoder RNN architecture used in the sentiment classification model is identical to the encoder RNN architecture of the dialog (tweet-reply) model as described in the paper.
Must specify that the sentiment classifier produces its final predictions via a fully connected (feed-forward) layer applied on top of the encoder representation.
Must specify that a softmax function is applied to the output of the fully connected layer to obtain a probability distribution over sentiment classes.

Must extract these architectural details from the section of the paper that defines the sentiment classification model (e.g., the 'Model', 'Classification Model', or equivalent architecture description section), not from unrelated sections such as introduction or experiments.
Must indicate that the model outputs a probability distribution specifically over multiple sentiment classes (e.g., positive/negative/neutral), not a single scalar score.

decisions: How is the dialog model pretrained and selected during training for the sentiment classification task?

requirements.description: Must state that the model undergoes a pretraining phase specifically using dialog data (tweet-reply or unlabeled dialog pairs) before sentiment classification fine-tuning.
Must describe that during pretraining the validation cost (or validation loss) is evaluated multiple times within each epoch, rather than only once per epoch.
Must specify the exact frequency of validation cost evaluation as 10 times per epoch during model pretraining.
Must explain that the model selected for subsequent use is the one with the best (lowest) validation cost among all evaluations, i.e., model selection is based on minimum validation cost.

Must identify and draw from the experimental setup or training procedure section that describes the dialog model pretraining and validation strategy, not from unrelated sections such as introduction or related work.

decisions: How does the paper describe the experimental setup and training behavior of the sentiment classification models, including data sizes, runs, evaluation metric, training duration, and convergence differences between pretrained and from-scratch models?

requirements.description: Must state that classifier model training is performed using labeled sentiment data, as described in the experimental setup section for training the sentiment classifier.
Must specify that 5 different training data sizes are applied for each method, matching the description of varying dataset sizes in the classifier training procedure section.
Must report that for each method and each data size, 5 runs are conducted with different random seeds, as detailed in the experimental protocol for repeated trials.
Must indicate that evaluation is based on the average of F-measure (F1) scores over the multiple runs, as defined in the evaluation metrics subsection.

Must describe that training duration is adjusted so that the cost (loss) converges, and that pretrained models converge very quickly while models trained from scratch converge slowly, as reported in the training behavior or convergence analysis part of the experiments.

decisions: What is the name of the proposed method introduced in the paper and how is it labeled on the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces a specific proposed method named "Dial" for pretraining sentiment classifiers with unlabeled dialog (tweet-reply) data.
Must retrieve the section or passage in the paper where the authors explicitly introduce and name the proposed method as "Dial" (e.g., in a 'Proposed Method' or method-introduction section).
Must state that the slide title or heading corresponding to the method introduction is exactly "The proposed method: Dial".
Must retrieve from the paper the conference identification information that the work was presented at the 56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics.
Must correctly extract and report the conference location and dates as "15-20 July 2018, Melbourne" as shown on the slide.

decisions: What baseline methods using LSTM RNNs does the paper define for sentiment classification pretraining and comparison?

requirements.description: Must identify that one baseline is an LSTM RNN model directly trained only on the labeled sentiment data (no unsupervised pretraining).
Must state that one baseline pretrains an LSTM-RNN as a language model before fine-tuning for sentiment classification.
Must state that another baseline pretrains an LSTM-RNN as a sequence autoencoder before fine-tuning for sentiment classification.

Must describe the construction of large-scale pseudo-labeled training data using emoji and emoticon-based distant supervision (i.e., preparing datasets utilizing emoticons or emoji as sentiment labels).
Must specify that some baselines pretrain models directly as sentiment classifiers using the pseudo-labeled emoji/emoticon data before applying them to the target sentiment task.

decisions: How does the paper define the baseline setup using linear models for sentiment classification, including data, preprocessing, and token set?

requirements.description: Must state that the baseline with linear models is trained using only the labeled sentiment data (i.e., without any unlabeled dialog/tweet-reply pretraining data).
Must specify that text segmentation/tokenization for the baseline is performed using MeCab, described in the paper as a de facto standard morphological analyzer.
Must mention that the baseline feature space explicitly includes an additional set of 233 emoji and emoticon tokens on top of the standard segmented text features.

Must identify and draw from the section that describes the baseline linear models (e.g., 'Baselines', 'Baseline with Linear Models', or equivalent experimental setup subsection), not from sections describing the proposed encoder-decoder pretraining method.
Must correctly attribute the work to the 56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2018), held 15–20 July 2018 in Melbourne, as stated in the paper's metadata.

decisions: How does the proposed dialog-based pretraining method affect F-measure performance compared to the default baseline across different numbers of training records?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison is between a default sentiment classifier and a classifier pretrained using unlabeled dialog (tweet-reply) data via an encoder-decoder (dialog) model.
Must retrieve the F-measure values for both the default model and the dialog-pretrained model from the results section (table or figure) that reports performance versus number of training records.

Must describe or reconstruct the figure or table that plots or lists F-measure as a function of the number of training records, including separate curves/columns for 'Default' and 'Dial' (dialog-pretrained) models.
Must use information from the experimental results section that specifically analyzes model performance under varying sizes of labeled training data (e.g., different '# of training records').

Must state the direction of the performance difference in F-measure (i.e., whether the dialog-pretrained model outperforms or underperforms the default model) for at least one specified number of training records.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s main conclusion about the effectiveness and future directions of the proposed pretraining strategy using paired dialog data for sentiment analysis?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper concludes the proposed pretraining strategy uses paired dialog data (e.g., tweet–reply pairs or dialog pairs) specifically for sentiment analysis.
Must report that the authors conclude this pretraining strategy is particularly or even more effective in extremely low-resource (very limited labeled data) situations.

Must indicate that the future work or conclusion section proposes exploring combinations of a large-scale unlabeled dataset with a supervised sentiment classification task (i.e., joint or staged use of unlabeled and labeled data).
Must mention that the authors propose, in their conclusion or future directions, exploiting other kinds of structures beyond the specific paired dialog data used in the current study.

Must identify that these points (effectiveness of the pretraining strategy, low-resource advantage, large-scale unlabeled plus supervised combination, and exploiting other structures) are drawn from the paper’s conclusion or closing discussion section rather than from intermediate technical sections.

decisions: Does the summary correctly identify and describe the paper’s use of dependency trees/forests for Japanese in KyotoEBMT, including their properties and limitations?

requirements.description: Must state that KyotoEBMT uses syntactic dependency analysis (dependency trees or forests) rather than constituent trees as the primary structural representation for translation.
Must explicitly mention that this dependency-based representation is considered the most natural or appropriate for Japanese in the system description.
Must describe that the chosen dependency representation is intended to preserve or contain all important semantic information from the input sentence.
Must note that the approach still relies on a few language-specific rules, indicating that the system is not entirely language-independent.

Must indicate that the dependency-based x-to-x variant used in KyotoEBMT is less commonly used than constituent-tree-based approaches and is sensitive to the parsing quality of both source and target languages.

decisions: How does the KyotoEBMT system pipeline process data from parallel corpus preparation through input sentence handling and tuning/reranking?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the section (or subsection) that outlines the overall KyotoEBMT system pipeline or architecture, including the ordered stages from corpus preparation to decoding and tuning.

Must extract the description of the 'preprocessing of the parallel corpus' stage, including that it is explicitly applied to a parallel corpus and is treated as an initial step in the KyotoEBMT pipeline.

Must extract the description of the 'processing of input sentence' stage as a distinct pipeline step that occurs after corpus preprocessing and refers specifically to handling a single input sentence at translation time.
Must identify that tuning and reranking of translation candidates are performed using kbMira, explicitly naming 'kbMira' as the optimization or tuning method used in the system.

Must retrieve the comparative statement that kbMira works better than PRO for this system, explicitly mentioning that kbMira outperforms PRO (or 'seems to work better than PRO for us') in the reported experiments.

decisions: What specific implementation characteristics and advantages of KyotoEBMT’s on-the-fly, flexible translation rules does the paper describe?

requirements.description: Must state that in KyotoEBMT all translation rules are computed on-the-fly for each input constituent (or input segment), rather than being precomputed and stored as a fixed rule list.

Must describe that on-the-fly rule computation provides full input context for computing features, explicitly linking this to the computation of significance and/or sparse features and noting that this makes feature computation more complicated and potentially slower.

Must explain that there is no limit on the size of matched rules due to the on-the-fly approach, and that this enables the possibility of outputting a perfect translation when the input is very similar to an example in the bilingual database.
Must identify that the system supports flexible rules with optional words and alternative insertion positions, contrasting these with a long list of separate alternative rules.

Must report that the decoder can process flexible rules more efficiently than a long list of alternative rules, and that some flexible rules may effectively encode more than millions of standard rules, emphasizing the efficiency/compactness claim made in the paper.

decisions: How does the KyotoEBMT system create flexible translation rules on-the-fly from an example sentence, including handling optional and ambiguously inserted words?

requirements.description: Must identify and state that the system supports 'flexible translation rule created on-the-fly' (or equivalent phrasing) as a core mechanism for example-based translation.
Must describe that the flexible rule is extracted from a concrete example sentence containing the phrase 'at present X(plastic) is Y(for example) produced Y(for example)'.
Must explain the role of variable X as a 'simple case' where X has a direct equivalent in the source example (i.e., X is aligned straightforwardly between source and target).
Must explain the role of variable Y as an 'ambiguous insertion position', indicating that Y marks positions where insertions can occur with multiple possible placements.

Must retrieve and state that the word 'raw' is null-aligned and therefore treated as optional (e.g., 'raw: null-aligned -> optional', and/or 'raw* petroleum' encoding many translation options at once, including 'Y(for example) optional word').

decisions: What specific implementation characteristics and advantages of KyotoEBMT’s on-the-fly, flexible translation rule computation does the paper describe?

requirements.description: Must state that in KyotoEBMT all translation rules are computed on-the-fly for each input (or input constituent), rather than being precomputed and stored as a fixed rule list.
Must describe that this on-the-fly rule computation can be slower and makes computing significance and sparse features more complicated, as explicitly noted in the paper.

Must explain that on-the-fly computation provides full context for computing features and imposes no limit on the size of matched rules, enabling the possibility of perfect translation when the input is very similar to an example.
Must identify the notion of flexible rules that support optional words and alternative insertion positions, as contrasted with a long list of separate alternative rules.

Must report that the decoder can process these flexible rules more efficiently than a long list of alternative rules and that some flexible rules may encode more than millions of standard rules, as quantified in the paper.

decisions: What specific architectural and training improvements were made to the KyotoEBMT system since the previous workshop, and how do they relate to parsing, alignment, features, neural components, and evaluation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the previous use of single input trees was replaced or extended with support for parse forests, explicitly mentioning forest-based parsing (e.g., "parse forests" or "forest Juman/KNP parses").

Must describe the alignment improvement pipeline by stating that alignments were originally corrected using syntactic dependency trees (citing or paraphrasing the Nakazawa and Kurohashi 2012 method) and are now further improved with additional mechanisms.

Must enumerate the newly introduced features for alignment and scoring, including (1) an explicit alignment score feature, (2) a context similarity score based on word2vec vectors, and (3) an RNNLM-based language model feature.
Must state that a neural machine translation (Neural MT) based reranking or component was added to the KyotoEBMT framework, distinguishing it from the previous non-neural configuration.

Must report that the system employs automatic nightly testing to monitor variations in BLEU scores and assertion errors (and/or memory leaks), and that overall improvements across all components are observed, even if the exact contribution of each element is hard to estimate.

decisions: How does the KyotoEBMT system use forest-based input to address limitations of tree-to-tree machine translation, and how is this implemented in terms of parse selection and encoding?

requirements.description: Must state that replacing single input trees with forests is presented as a (partial) solution to issues of Tree-to-Tree machine translation.
Must specify that the system uses 20-best input parses (an n-best list of parses) as the basis for constructing the forest.
Must explain that forest-based input is intended to help with parsing errors and syntactic divergences between source and target languages.
Must describe that the n-best parses for all inputs are merged and reranked to form the forest representation.
Must mention that an exponential number of input parses can be encoded in the forest and that the final selection of parses is performed during decoding.

decisions: How does the KyotoEBMT system improve word alignment, and what specific tools and parsing resources are used in its alignment pipeline?

requirements.description: Must state that the system uses Nile (Riesa et al., 2011) specifically to improve the alignment, as suggested by Neubig and Duh (2014).
Must state that using Nile requires parsing into constituent trees in addition to the existing dependency trees.
Must identify the Ckylark parser (Oda et al., 2015) as the tool used to obtain constituent trees for Japanese.
Must identify the Berkeley Parser as the tool used to obtain constituent trees for Chinese and English.

Must describe the alignment pipeline as consisting of three elements: Giza++, Kurohashi (Nakazawa, 2012), and Nile, and must mention that Nile is the third element combined with dependency and constituent trees.

decisions: How does the KyotoEBMT system integrate a bilingual neural network language model with EBMT, and what are the observed character-level BLEU effects for Japanese–Chinese translation and reranking?

requirements.description: Must state that the KyotoEBMT system combines a neural machine translation (Neural MT) model with the example-based MT (EBMT) framework, explicitly describing the neural component as a bilingual neural network language model conditioned on the input (following Bahdanau et al., 2015).

Must describe that Japanese and Chinese are processed as sequences of characters (character-based modeling) in the bilingual neural network, and must explicitly mention that this choice is motivated by avoiding segmentation issues and enabling faster training.

Must reference and correctly interpret the figure/plot showing 'Reranked BLEU / NeuralMT char-BLEU vs Epochs for J->C', including that the x-axis corresponds to training epochs and that both the neural MT character BLEU and the reranked BLEU curves are plotted for Japanese-to-Chinese translation.

Must report that neural MT models used alone produced poor translations, specifically that the character BLEU score for Chinese-to-Japanese (C->J) with pure neural MT is approximately half of the KyotoEBMT system's character BLEU for the same direction.

Must state that reranking performance (measured by BLEU when using the bilingual neural network as a reranker) saturates before the standalone neural MT model's performance saturates, and must distinguish between the three curves/metrics: Neural MT cBLEU, reranked BLEU, and KyotoEBMT cBLEU.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the reported WAT2015 evaluation results, especially the BLEU/RIBES changes and the effect of reranking for different Japanese–Chinese directions?

requirements.description: Must identify the WAT2015 results section or table where BLEU scores are reported for Japanese↔Chinese (JC and CJ) translation directions and extract the numerical or described improvement that is approximately +4 BLEU after the system improvements.
