decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s theoretical approach based on assuming Zipf’s law and its analogy to physics when constructing trade-off formulas?

requirements.description: Must state that the theoretical analysis explicitly assumes the corpus word frequency distribution follows Zipf's law (a power-law distribution).
Must describe Zipf's law as an empirical rule capturing the long-tail property of word frequencies in a corpus (i.e., many low-frequency words).

Must explain that the methodology is to construct a theory by taking an empirically observed regularity (Zipf's law) as given, analogous to how physics uses experimentally observed constants (e.g., gravitational acceleration g).

Must include the specific physics analogy that, by believing in a fixed gravity acceleration g, one can theoretically derive the landing point of a ball, and relate this to deriving trade-off relationships in the paper.
Must explicitly connect the use of Zipf's law to the goal of clarifying trade-off relationships between perplexity and reduced vocabulary size in the proposed theory.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the paper’s use of Zipf’s law to characterize word frequency distributions in corpora, as presented on the Zipf’s law slide?

requirements.description: Must state that Zipf's law is an empirical rule observed on real text corpora and explicitly attribute it to Zipf (1935) or an equivalent citation from the paper.
Must state that under Zipf's law, a word's frequency is inversely proportional to its rank in the frequency list (i.e., f(w) ∝ 1/r(w)).
Must extract or reconstruct the mathematical form of Zipf's law used in the paper, including a constant C and the relationship f(w) = C / r(w) (or an equivalent notation mapping C, f(w), and r(w)).
Must describe that the paper represents Zipf's law using a log-log graph where word frequency is plotted against frequency rank and appears approximately as a straight (linear) line.
Must mention that the visualization contrasts a Zipf-distributed curve with a 'random' or non-Zipf distribution on the same frequency vs. rank log-log plot, as indicated in the slide text.

decisions: How does the paper define and interpret perplexity (PP) as an evaluation measure for statistical language models?

requirements.description: Must state that perplexity (PP) is a widely used evaluation measure of statistical models, specifically in the context of language or probabilistic models.
Must define perplexity as the geometric mean of the inverse of the per-word likelihood (or equivalently, the exponentiated average negative log-likelihood) computed on a held-out test corpus.
Must explicitly mention that the perplexity is computed on a held-out test corpus, not on the training data.
Must explain the intuitive interpretation that perplexity corresponds to how many possibilities one effectively has for estimating or predicting each word.
Must state the directional relationship that lower perplexity indicates better generalization performance of the model.

decisions: How does the paper model or approximate the probabilities of words that are removed when reducing the vocabulary of a corpus?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces an approach where the probabilities of all removed (low-frequency) words are treated or inferred as a single constant value rather than distinct probabilities.
Must describe that this constant probability for removed words is chosen or derived so as to approximate the probability distribution that would have been learned from the original, unreduced corpus.

Must link the constant-probability treatment of removed words specifically to the theoretical tradeoff formulas for perplexity under vocabulary reduction (e.g., in the derivation for k-gram models or topic models).

Must identify and use the part of the paper where the authors explicitly define how probabilities of excluded or low-frequency words are handled after vocabulary reduction (e.g., the modeling or assumptions subsection of the theoretical framework).

Must mention that the constant-probability approximation for removed words is evaluated or validated by comparing perplexity (or related metrics) between the reduced-vocabulary model and the model trained on the original corpus, on either synthetic or real corpora.

decisions: How does the paper define and derive the predictive distribution and perplexity behavior of unigram language models on reduced corpora under vocabulary reduction?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide concerns unigram (1-gram) language models specifically, and not k-gram models in general, by referencing the part of the paper that treats the unigram case separately from higher-order k-grams.

Must state that the predictive distribution for the unigram model is expressed in terms of word frequencies f(w), probabilities p(w), and total token count N, as given in the paper's unigram formulation (e.g., p(w) = f(w)/N or its reduced-corpus analogue).

Must describe that the restored probability p̂(w) for words after vocabulary reduction is substituted into the perplexity (PP) expression, and that a constant parameter (e.g., a scaling or smoothing constant) is optimized by minimizing perplexity with respect to this constant, as explicitly derived in the unigram section.

Must retrieve and distinguish the variables representing original vocabulary size and reduced vocabulary size (e.g., V and V′ or equivalent notation) from the paper's notation, and indicate that perplexity is analyzed as a function of reduced corpus size and reduced vocabulary size.

Must draw from the specific part of the paper that analyzes perplexity of unigram models under reduced corpora (the unigram-specific subsection or derivation), rather than from sections dealing with topic models or general k-gram models.

decisions: What does the paper state about the form of the perplexity PP1 of the optimal restored distribution of a unigram model for any reduced vocabulary size W?

requirements.description: Must state that the result concerns a unigram language model, explicitly identifying it as a 'unigram model' (or 1-gram model) rather than higher-order k-grams.
Must state that the perplexity under discussion is PP1 of the 'optimal restored distribution' (or equivalent phrasing that clearly indicates the restored distribution after vocabulary reduction).
Must specify that the theorem or result is stated for an arbitrary or generic reduced vocabulary size denoted by W (e.g., 'for any reduced vocabulary size W').
Must identify that the expression or formula for PP1 takes the form of a Bertrand series, and must explicitly use the term 'Bertrand series' or an unambiguous equivalent.

Must attribute this statement to a formal result (e.g., a theorem, proposition, or named result such as 'Theorem PP') in the paper that characterizes PP1 for unigram models under vocabulary reduction.

decisions: How does the paper approximate the perplexity of unigram models when low-frequency words are removed, and what is the functional form and behavior of the resulting approximation?

requirements.description: Must state that the entropy H(X) and the branching factor B(X) for unigrams are approximated by definite integrals rather than discrete sums, explicitly linking this to the unigram perplexity approximation.

Must identify and describe the approximate formula for unigram perplexity (or its underlying entropy/branching factor) that is derived from the integral approximation, referring to it as an explicit closed-form or simplified expression (the 'approximate formula o').

Must state that the derived approximate formula for unigram perplexity (or its proxy) is quasi-polynomial and specifically characterized as quadratic in the relevant variable (e.g., vocabulary size or cutoff threshold).
Must state that when plotted on a log-log graph, the approximate unigram perplexity formula behaves as a quadratic function (i.e., exhibits quadratic behavior in log-log space).

Must attribute these properties (integral approximation of H(X) and B(X), the quasi-polynomial/quadratic formula, and its log-log quadratic behavior) specifically to the part of the paper that analyzes unigram models or 'PP of unigrams', distinguishing it from k-gram or topic model analyses.

decisions: How does the paper use real Reuters data to analyze unigram perplexity as vocabulary size is reduced, and what conclusion does it draw about the role of the theoretical model?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the specific figure that plots unigram perplexity versus reduced vocabulary size for the real Reuters corpus on a log-log scale (e.g., a log-log graph labeled or described as using Reuters data).

Must state that the real-corpus experiment is conducted on a dataset with the same size as Reuters, or explicitly that the corpus used is the Reuters corpus (or an equivalent description given in the paper).

Must explicitly mention that the theoretical analysis is primarily used to infer or predict the growth rate (scaling behavior) of perplexity as vocabulary size is reduced, rather than to match the absolute perplexity values.

Must report that, when comparing theory to the real Reuters-based log-log perplexity plot, the agreement is characterized in terms of the slope or growth rate, with a noted discrepancy in exact perplexity values.

Must draw from the section or subsection where the authors compare theoretical predictions to real-corpus (Reuters) experiments on unigram models, not from synthetic-corpus or higher-order k-gram/topic-model sections.

decisions: How does the paper define and justify the simple k-gram model used to study perplexity under a Zipfian random word sequence, including its key illustrative bigram properties and its relation to real corpora?

requirements.description: Must state that the k-gram model is defined on a random word sequence whose word probabilities follow Zipf's law (i.e., k-grams are calculated from a Zipfian random sequence, not from a structured natural language model).
Must explicitly characterize the k-gram model as a deliberately oversimplified or 'stupid' baseline model used for theoretical analysis of perplexity on reduced vocabularies.

Must describe the specific illustrative bigram property that the bigram 'is is' (or an equivalent repeated high-frequency word bigram) is predicted to be quite frequent under the model due to Zipfian word frequencies.

Must describe the specific illustrative bigram property that two distinct bigrams composed of the same two high-frequency words in different orders (e.g., 'is a' and 'a is') have the same expected frequency under the model.

Must mention that later experiments in the paper compare this simple Zipf-based k-gram model to real corpora and find that it can roughly capture the observed behavior of real data with respect to perplexity or n-gram statistics.

decisions: How does the paper formally define the frequency of a k-gram and the associated decay functions g₂ and g_k, including the role of the Piltz divisor function?

requirements.description: Must state the formal definition of the frequency f_k of a k-gram w_k exactly as given in the paper (i.e., as a function that maps a specific k-gram w_k to its frequency in the corpus, using the same notation f_k and w_k).
Must provide the explicit mathematical expression for the decay function g_2 of bigrams, using the same symbol g_2 and the same variables/parameters as defined in the paper.

Must provide the explicit mathematical definition of the general decay function g_k for k-grams, including how it is constructed or defined "through" another function or summation as specified in the paper.

Must identify and name the Piltz divisor function exactly as used in the paper and state that it represents the number of divisors of an integer n (i.e., "# of divisors of n" or equivalent precise wording).

Must extract all definitions and formulas related to f_k, g_2, g_k, and the Piltz divisor function from the same definitional or theoretical section where k-gram frequency and decay functions are introduced, not from experimental or results sections.

decisions: How does the paper define and estimate the exponent of k-gram frequency distributions under a power-law assumption?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper assumes k-gram frequencies follow a power-law distribution (Zipf-like) over ranks r.
Must report that prior work [Ha+ 2006] found that k-gram frequencies roughly follow a power law with an exponent smaller than 1.
Must describe that the paper defines an 'optimal exponent' k for k-gram distributions within its model based on the power-law assumption.
Must explain that the optimal exponent k is obtained by minimizing the sum of squared errors between the inverse gradients g_k^{-1}(r) and r^{1/k} on a log-log graph.

Must identify and draw from the specific section where the paper discusses the exponent of k-gram distributions and its estimation procedure (the section that introduces g_k, its inverse, and the fitting on a log-log plot).

decisions: How does the paper formally express the perplexity of the optimal restored distribution of a k-gram model as a function of the reduced vocabulary size W, and how are the resulting series characterized (e.g., as hyper harmonic or Bertrand series)?

requirements.description: Must identify the specific part of the paper where the perplexity of the optimal restored distribution of a k-gram model is defined as a function of the reduced vocabulary size W (i.e., a corollary or theorem explicitly tying perplexity to W).

Must extract the exact mathematical expression for the perplexity of the optimal restored distribution of a k-gram model, including the summation form (e.g., a series over x with exponent a) that appears in the corollary corresponding to the slide.
Must capture the identification of the derived perplexity expression as a hyper harmonic series, including the notation that matches the form '∑ x^{-a}' or equivalent as described in the paper.
Must capture the identification of a related or transformed expression involving '∑ x^{-a} ln x' (or equivalent) as a Bertrand series, explicitly using the term 'Bertrand series' as in the paper.

Must reference the specific corollary or subsection where the paper names and classifies these series (hyper harmonic series and Bertrand series) in the context of k-gram model perplexity under reduced vocabulary size.

decisions: What assumptions does the paper state are needed when analyzing the perplexity of higher-order k-gram models as a function of reduced vocabulary size?

requirements.description: Must identify that the discussion concerns perplexity of k-gram language models specifically in the context of reduced vocabulary size (i.e., after removing low-frequency words).
Must state that the paper explicitly assumes the use of backoff when dealing with higher-order k-gram models in the theoretical analysis.
Must state that the paper explicitly assumes the use of smoothing when dealing with higher-order k-gram models in the theoretical analysis.

Must attribute these assumptions (backoff and smoothing for higher-order k-grams) to the part of the paper where the authors derive or discuss the tradeoff formulae for perplexity of k-gram models under reduced vocabularies (e.g., the theoretical analysis or model formulation section).

decisions: What additional theoretical properties related to power-law behavior and coupon collector analysis does the paper present for corpus size and k-gram coverage?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper treats the problem as a variant of the coupon collector's problem, specifically in the context of collecting all k-grams (or coupons) from a corpus.
Must state that the occurrence probabilities of coupons (words or k-grams) are assumed to follow a stable distribution consistent with a power law (Zipf-like) distribution.

Must retrieve the theoretical result that gives the corpus size (number of trials) required to collect all k-grams, expressed as a function of k and vocabulary size W, including the explicit case distinction of the form 'when k ≲ W ln W, otherwise k ≳ ...' or equivalent threshold condition involving W ln W.

Must extract the formulas or inequalities that provide lower and upper bounds on the number of distinct k-grams observed as a function of corpus size N and vocabulary size W (i.e., bounds of the form: lower bound ≤ #k-grams ≤ upper bound, parameterized by N and W).

Must locate and use the specific section or subsection where the paper discusses 'additional properties' or power-law-based coupon collector analysis (e.g., the part that cites prior works on power law distributions and derives corpus-size/k-gram relationships), rather than only using the main perplexity tradeoff formulas.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize how perplexity is defined for topic models by describing the LDA framework, its inference method, and the meanings of the key latent variables and parameters?

requirements.description: Must identify Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) as the specific topic model used to define perplexity, explicitly naming it and citing Blei et al. (2003) as the source model.
Must state that the learning/inference procedure for LDA is performed using Gibbs sampling and explicitly associate this with Griffiths & Steyvers (2004).
Must describe that the inference goal is to obtain a good topic assignment z_i for each word w_i in the corpus (i.e., one latent topic variable per token).
Must state that the model involves posterior distributions over two hidden parameter types: (1) mixture rates of topics in each document and (2) occurrence rates of words in each topic.

Must correctly interpret the two posterior parameter types as (1) the mixture rate of topic z in document d and (2) the occurrence rate of word w in topic z, using document index d, topic index z, and word index w consistently with the paper's notation.

decisions: What simplifying assumptions about topic-wise word distributions and document-topic configurations does the paper introduce to theoretically analyze perplexity under Zipfian vocabularies?

requirements.description: Must state that the word distribution of each topic (the topic-specific word distribution) is assumed to follow Zipf's law, explicitly treating each topic as if it were a corpus.

Must identify that the analysis is based on two extreme-case assumptions about document-topic mixtures, explicitly naming or describing both 'Case All' (each document evenly has all topics) and 'Case One' (each document only has one topic with a uniform distribution over topics).
Must state that the actual perplexity curve of the topic model is expected to lie between the perplexity values derived for the two extreme cases ('Case All' and 'Case One').
Must explain that in the 'Case All' setting, the perplexity of the topic model reduces to (or equals) the perplexity of a unigram model.
Must mention that under the 'Case All' assumption, the marginal predictive distribution used for perplexity computation is independent of the document index d.

decisions: How is the perplexity of the optimal restored distribution of an LDA topic model defined in Case One for any reduced vocabulary size W, and what does T represent in this theorem?

requirements.description: Must state that the theorem concerns the perplexity of the optimal restored distribution of a topic model (LDA) under "Case One" for a reduced vocabulary of size W.

Must identify that the result is a theorem (often labeled or described as a theorem in the text) giving a closed-form or explicit formula for perplexity as a function of the reduced vocabulary size W in the LDA setting.
Must explicitly mention that W denotes the reduced vocabulary size used in the corpus after low-frequency word removal, as assumed in the Zipf-based analysis.
Must explicitly identify that T in the theorem denotes the number of topics in the LDA model (e.g., "T: # of topics in LDA").

Must retrieve the specific part of the paper where "Case One" for LDA/topic models is defined or introduced, and use that definition to correctly contextualize the perplexity formula (i.e., not confuse it with other cases or with k-gram models).

decisions: What does the paper report about memory usage and computational time when using a 1/10-sized reduced corpus on the Reuters dataset for LDA learning?

requirements.description: Must identify that the reported results concern LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation) learning on the Reuters corpus specifically, not another dataset or model.

Must retrieve the quantitative comparison that the memory usage of the reduced '(1/10)-corpus' is approximately 60% of that of the full corpus (or equivalent baseline) as stated in the paper (e.g., from a results table or text).

Must recognize that the '(1/10)-corpus' refers to a corpus reduced in size (e.g., by removing low-frequency words or subsampling to one-tenth) and that this reduction is the experimental condition being evaluated for memory and time tradeoffs.

Must state that the reduced '(1/10)-corpus' configuration enables in-memory computing for larger corpora (i.e., fits in memory more easily than the full corpus), as explicitly claimed in the paper's discussion of the Reuters results.

Must report that the computational time for LDA learning on the '(1/10)-corpus' decreased only slightly (i.e., the time reduction is small or limited) relative to the full Reuters corpus, as described in the corresponding results section, figure, or table.

decisions: What main theoretical and empirical conclusions does the paper draw about the trade-off between vocabulary cutoff and perplexity in k-gram and topic models under Zipf’s law?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper derives trade-off formulae for the cutoff strategy specifically for both k-gram language models and topic models, assuming the corpus follows Zipf's law.

Must explicitly describe the relationship "perplexity vs. reduced vocabulary size" as a central theoretical object, i.e., that perplexity is analyzed as a function of the reduced vocabulary size after removing low-frequency words.

Must report that experiments on real corpora were used to validate the theory and that these experiments showed the estimated perplexity growth rate (from the theoretical formulae) is reasonably accurate.

Must explain that an optimal cutoff parameter can be selected by maximizing the vocabulary reduction rate subject to a constraint on keeping perplexity within an acceptable relative increase (i.e., an acceptable relative perplexity).

Must mention that the authors discuss the possibility of theoretically deriving empirical parameters or rules of thumb for NLP tasks based on Zipf's law, and pose the question of deriving further such rules of thumb from Zipfian assumptions.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper’s motivation for modeling valence and arousal using a circumplex (dimensional) model rather than traditional product-focused, discrete-emotion sentiment analysis?

requirements.description: Must identify and state the paper’s contrast between product-oriented sentiment (opinions towards products, restaurants, events, etc.) and affective states about self or others as distinct targets for modeling.

Must explicitly mention that models of product sentiment and models of emotion/affective state are argued in the paper to "should be different" or otherwise clearly distinguished in purpose and design.

Must retrieve the discussion of discrete emotion models in NLP, including explicit reference to Ekman’s six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise) as the most popular discrete scheme.

Must describe the dimensional model of affect used in the paper, including that each affective state is represented as a combination of real-valued components and that the most popular such model is the circumplex model of affect.

Must identify that the circumplex model in this paper is instantiated via two independent neurophysiological dimensions/components: valence (or sentiment) and arousal, and that some emotions can share similar lexical cues (e.g., words like "hell", "bad" appearing in sadness, fear, anger).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and attribute the circumplex model of affect / emotion circumplex source as presented in the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper situates valence and arousal within the circumplex model of affect (i.e., a 2D space with valence and arousal axes).
Must reference the specific figure or diagram in the paper that depicts the circumplex model of affect or emotion circumplex (e.g., a 2D circular layout with valence and arousal).

Must retrieve the external source citation associated with the circumplex/emotion model figure, specifically the work by Jonker & Van der Merwe on emotion episodes of Afrikaans-speaking employees in the workplace, if it appears in the paper's figure caption or references.

Must cover the section or subsection where the circumplex model of affect is introduced or defined (e.g., background, theory, or affective model description) and extract the associated source attribution for the model or figure.
Must explain that posts are positioned in the circumplex space using two separate ordinal nine-point scales for valence and arousal, linking this scaling explicitly to the circumplex model of affect.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s described applications of modelling valence and arousal for large-scale psychological studies and related analyses?

requirements.description: Must state that one key application proposed in the paper is automated, large-scale psychological studies using social media posts to track mood over time.
Must specify that the paper mentions measuring mood variations by time-of-day and day-of-week as an explicit application of the valence–arousal model.
Must mention that the paper discusses clinical or pathological applications, explicitly including bipolar disorder and schizophrenic breaks as example use cases.
Must identify that the paper proposes analysing emotion content in narrative media, explicitly including movies and books, as an application of the model.
Must describe that the paper suggests correlating inferred emotional states with external factors, explicitly including examples such as weather and sports game outcomes.

decisions: How does the paper define and scale the valence and arousal dimensions used to annotate Facebook posts?

requirements.description: Must state that valence is treated as sentiment or polarity, explicitly using the phrasing 'valence (or sentiment or polarity)' or an equivalent parenthetical clarification from the paper.
Must specify that valence is annotated on a nine-point ordinal scale ranging from 1 to 9, as defined in the dataset description.
Must report the semantic anchors for the valence scale: 1 corresponding to 'very negative', 5 corresponding to 'neutral/objective', and 9 corresponding to 'very positive', as given in the paper.
Must identify arousal as a separate dimension from valence, representing intensity, consistent with the circumplex model of affect described in the paper.

Must report that arousal is also annotated on a nine-point ordinal scale, with 1 corresponding to a 'neutral/objective post' and 9 corresponding to 'very high intensity', as defined in the annotation scheme.

decisions: What examples does the paper provide of Facebook posts annotated with average valence (V) and arousal (A) ratings?

requirements.description: Must state that the examples are Facebook (or Social Media) posts annotated with average valence (V) and arousal (A) ratings, explicitly naming both valence and arousal.

Must describe that the slide (or corresponding figure/example block in the paper) shows raw text snippets of posts followed by a caption indicating they are annotated with average valence (V) and arousal (A) ratings.
Must retrieve and include the example post text beginning with "Is the one whoz GOing to Light Up your" as shown in the paper.
Must retrieve and include the example post text "Blessed with a baby boy today ... the boring life is back :( ..." as shown in the paper.

Must retrieve and include the example post text "IS SUPER STRESSED AND ITS JUST THE SEC- OND MONTH OF SCHOOL ..D:" (including the line break in "SEC- OND" or an equivalent hyphenation) as shown in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper define the sampling constraints for the Facebook messages used to construct the dataset (in terms of user distinctness and time interval)?

requirements.description: Must state that, by design of the dataset, each Facebook message in the corpus is taken from a distinct user (i.e., no user contributes more than one message).

Must describe the sampling procedure or corpus construction step where the authors specify that all collected messages come from the same defined time interval (e.g., a fixed date range or contiguous period).
Must extract the two sampling constraints (distinct user per message and common time interval) from the dataset description or data collection section where the Facebook posts corpus is introduced.
Must make clear that the 'distinct user' and 'same time interval' constraints are properties of the dataset composition, not properties of the valence/arousal annotation procedure.

decisions: How were Facebook posts annotated for valence and arousal, and under what conditions were messages deemed un-ratable?

requirements.description: Must state that the annotators were psychology students who received training specifically for annotating valence and arousal (or these affective traits).
Must describe that the training included an anchoring procedure (e.g., use of anchor examples or reference points) for the annotation scales.
Must specify that annotators were instructed to avoid distractions that might affect their mood during annotation, explicitly mentioning examples such as music.
Must report that messages were considered un-ratable if they were not written in English.
Must report that messages were considered un-ratable if they contained no cues relevant to valence or arousal (i.e., no affective cues).

decisions: What do the annotation results show about the distribution of average valence and arousal ratings and their correlation in the Facebook posts dataset?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the figure that presents histograms of the average rating scores for the annotated Facebook posts (i.e., distribution plots of average valence and average arousal).
Must state that the histograms concern average rating scores on the two nine-point ordinal scales corresponding specifically to valence and arousal.
Must report the numerical Pearson correlation (or equivalent correlation measure) between valence and arousal ratings as r = 0.085.
Must specify that the reported correlation r = 0.085 is computed after excluding or ignoring posts labeled as neutral.

Must draw the above information specifically from the part of the paper that reports annotation results or data analysis of the annotated ratings (e.g., the 'Annotation Results' or equivalent results section), not from dataset description or methodology-only sections.

decisions: How does the paper describe the variation in valence and arousal with age when the data is split by gender?

requirements.description: Must state that the analysis concerns how both valence and arousal vary as a function of age in the dataset (i.e., affective ratings plotted against age).
Must specify that a LOESS (locally weighted regression) fit is used to model or smooth the relationship between age and the valence/arousal ratings.
Must reference the figure or plot in the paper that shows valence and arousal as curves over age produced using a LOESS fit.
Must indicate that the underlying data for the visualization comes from the paper's Facebook post dataset annotated with valence and arousal scores.
Must mention that the visualization or discussion explicitly splits the data by gender into at least two groups: Male and Female.

decisions: How does the paper model and evaluate prediction of valence and arousal from Facebook posts?

requirements.description: Must state that valence and arousal are predicted as two separate target variables (i.e., separate prediction/classification/regression tasks).
Must specify that the input text representation uses a bag-of-words feature set restricted to unigrams only.
Must identify the prediction model as a linear regression model with elastic net regularization (not any other regression or classification algorithm).
Must mention that model evaluation is performed using 10-fold cross-validation (including the explicit number of folds).

decisions: What baseline lexicon resources and their key statistics does the paper use for modelling valence and arousal in Facebook posts?

requirements.description: Must identify that the listed resources are used as baseline models/lexicons for predicting valence and arousal (or sentiment) in the study, not as the main proposed method.
Must state that one baseline resource provides valence and arousal ratings for approximately 1400 words and is attributed to Bradley et al. (e.g., ANEW).
Must state that another baseline resource provides valence and arousal ratings for approximately 14,000 words and is attributed to Warriner et al.
Must state that a further baseline resource contains 7,629 words rated for positive or negative sentiment and is attributed to Wilson et al.
Must indicate that the Hashtag Sentiment Lexicon is used as a baseline and is specifically described as being adapted to Social Media.

decisions: Which models' message rating prediction accuracies (in Pearson r) are compared in the results of this paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the reported metric is message rating prediction accuracy measured using Pearson correlation coefficient (Pearson r), not another metric such as accuracy percentage or F1.
Must identify the specific result element (table or figure) where message rating prediction accuracy in Pearson r is reported for multiple models.
Must list ANEW as one of the models/feature sets whose message rating prediction accuracy (Pearson r) is reported.
Must list AffNorms, MPQA, and NRC as distinct models/lexicons whose message rating prediction accuracies (Pearson r) are reported.
Must list a BOW (bag-of-words) model as one of the compared models whose message rating prediction accuracy (Pearson r) is reported.

decisions: What does the paper report about the words most positively and negatively correlated with valence in Facebook posts, and how are their correlation strength and relative frequency represented?

requirements.description: Must identify that the discussed feature is word-level correlation with the valence dimension (not arousal or overall sentiment), explicitly linking the listed words to valence scores in the dataset.

Must retrieve from the paper the specific example words that are most positively correlated with valence, including at least the majority of: 'birthday', 'happy', 'thank', 'great', 'love', 'thanks', 'wishes', 'wonderful'.
Must retrieve from the paper at least one example of a word that is most negatively correlated with valence, specifically including 'hate' as a negatively correlated word.

Must describe or reference the figure or table in the paper that ranks words by their correlation with valence and indicates both correlation strength and relative frequency (e.g., a plot or table with two axes or columns for these measures).

Must state that the correlation values between words and valence were computed quantitatively (e.g., via correlation coefficients between word occurrence and valence ratings across posts), distinguishing correlation strength from relative frequency as two separate statistics.

decisions: Which specific words in the dataset are most positively and most negatively correlated with arousal, and how are their correlation strength and relative frequency represented?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide concerns lexical items (individual words) whose usage in Facebook posts is statistically associated with the arousal dimension of affect, not valence.

Must retrieve from the paper the specific example words shown as highly positively correlated with arousal, including at least 'birthday', 'happy', 'its', 'wishes', 'soooo', 'thanks', 'christmas', 'sunday', 'yay', 'status', 'life'.
Must retrieve from the paper the specific example words shown as highly negatively correlated with arousal, including at least 'people' and 'bored'.

Must describe the figure or table that lists words by their correlation with arousal and visually encodes both 'correlation strength' and 'relative frequency' for each word (e.g., via axes, bars, or markers).

Must state that the word–arousal associations are computed using a correlation measure (e.g., Pearson correlation) between word occurrence features and the annotated arousal scores in the Facebook posts.

decisions: How does the paper quantitatively position Facebook posts like 'bored', 'soooo excited', and 'yay' on the circumplex model of affect using valence and arousal ratings?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper models affective states using the circumplex model of affect with two dimensions: valence (sentiment) and arousal (intensity), each represented as separate ordinal nine-point scales.
Must state that the dataset consists of 2,895 social media (Facebook) posts annotated by two psychologically trained annotators with valence and arousal scores on the nine-point scales.

Must reference the specific figure or diagram in the paper that plots example posts on the circumplex model of affect and includes or is exemplified by posts such as 'bored', 'soooo excited', and 'yay' at different valence–arousal positions.

Must retrieve the example textual posts used in the circumplex illustration (e.g., 'bored', 'soooo excited', 'yay') from the paper, as they appear in the figure caption, example list, or descriptive text tied to the circumplex visualization.

Must cover the section that introduces and explains the circumplex-based quantitative analysis of posts (e.g., the section describing how posts are mapped into the valence–arousal space and illustrated with concrete example posts).

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and state the key takeaway that the paper provides an annotated Facebook dataset and an accompanying bag-of-words model?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces or provides an annotated Facebook (or Social Media) dataset of user posts, not just generic sentiment data.
Must specify that the annotations in the dataset concern affective dimensions (valence and arousal) rather than only generic sentiment polarity.
Must mention that the paper includes or makes available a bag-of-words model built from the annotated Facebook posts.

Must derive the availability of the dataset and bag-of-words model from content corresponding to contribution, resources, or dataset description sections (e.g., where the authors describe releasing or providing the data/model), not from unrelated methodological details.
Must correctly reflect that the dataset size is on the order of several thousand posts (approximately 2895 posts) if any size is mentioned when describing the annotated Facebook dataset.

decisions: How does the paper quantify and report agreement between the two annotators for each affective dimension in the new Facebook posts dataset?

requirements.description: Must retrieve the table that reports, for each dimension (valence and arousal), the individual rater (R1 and R2) mean and standard deviation scores.
Must identify that 'R1' and 'R2' refer to the two psychologically trained annotators who rated the Facebook posts on the nine-point scales.
Must extract the inter-annotator correlation (IA Corr.) values reported in the agreement table for each dimension.

Must locate and use the specific section that discusses annotator agreement or reliability (e.g., an 'Agreement', 'Annotation', or 'Inter-annotator Reliability' subsection) as the source for the slide content.
Must preserve the tabular structure with columns labeled 'Dimension', 'R1', 'R2', and 'IA Corr.' when summarizing or recreating the agreement information.

decisions: What contextual background and objectives does the paper present regarding semantic specialization of word embeddings and its relation to Retrofitting-based approaches?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper is concerned with the semantic specialization of word embeddings (i.e., modifying embeddings to better encode semantic similarity).
Must describe that most existing approaches to semantic specialization follow or are inspired by the Retrofitting method of Faruqui et al. (2015).
Must explain that these Retrofitting-style methods rely on an a priori set of lexical semantic relations (e.g., synonymy and other lexical relations) as external knowledge to guide specialization.

Must specify the core operation of Retrofitting-style methods: bringing word vectors closer together when they participate in similarity relations (such as synonymy) and pushing them farther apart when they participate in dissimilarity relations.
Must identify the paper's objective as improving word embeddings for semantic similarity without relying on an a priori lexical resource or external lexical semantic relations.

decisions: How does the paper define and use corpus splits and distributional representations to argue that bringing pseudo-sense representations of a word closer makes its embedding more general and better?

requirements.description: Must identify that the corpus C is explicitly split into two equal parts, denoted C1 and C2.
Must state that the distributional representation of a word w from a corpus C is denoted as distrepC(w).
Must specify that separate distributional representations distrepC1(w) and distrepC2(w) are constructed for the same word w from the two corpus parts C1 and C2.
Must report that the paper characterizes the differences between distrepC1(w) and distrepC2(w) as contingent (i.e., not essential to the word's meaning).
Must explain that the method involves bringing distrepC1(w) and distrepC2(w) closer to each other to obtain a more general and better representation of w.

decisions: How does the Pseudofit method implement pseudo-senses to obtain more general dense word representations from a single corpus?

requirements.description: Must state that dense word representations are obtained using the Skip-Gram model, explicitly citing Mikolov et al. (2013) as the underlying approach.

Must describe the baseline setup where 2 sub-corpora lead to 2 separate representation spaces, and that this configuration requires a projection into a shared space which is identified as a source of disturbances.
Must explain that Pseudofit instead uses 1 corpus but creates 2 (or more) pseudo-senses for each word by arbitrarily splitting the occurrences of each word into two or more subsets.
Must mention the generation of distributional contexts for pseudo-senses and the subsequent transformation of these pseudo-sense contexts into dense representations (i.e., pseudo-sense embeddings).
Must state that the convergence of the pseudo-word (pseudo-sense) representations is used to obtain a more general word representation for each word.

decisions: How does the paper define and construct representations of pseudo-words (pseudo-senses) for each word occurrence when building dense representations in Pseudofit?

requirements.description: Must state that each word is associated with 3 representations: 2 pseudo-senses plus the original word representation.
Must explain that 2 successive occurrences of the same word are assigned to 2 different pseudo-senses (i.e., alternating or separating occurrences into distinct pseudo-senses).

Must describe that for each occurrence, contexts are generated for the current pseudo-sense together with the word itself (i.e., context construction is conditioned on the active pseudo-sense plus the base word).

Must describe the 'frequency trick' as adding the base word representation in addition to pseudo-sense representations to avoid the impact of splitting occurrences roughly in half between the two pseudo-senses.
Must mention that these pseudo-sense and word representations are used to build dense representations of pseudo-words (pseudo-senses).

decisions: How does the paper describe the convergence of pseudo word representations when using PARAGRAM to specialize word embeddings with pseudo-senses?

requirements.description: Must state that each word w is associated with three representations: v as the original word embedding, and v1 and v2 as pseudo-sense embeddings, and that v, v1, and v2 are assumed to be semantically equivalent.

Must describe that a semantic specialization method is applied jointly to v, v1, and v2 using the similarity relations between these three representations (i.e., treating them as mutually similar during specialization).
Must identify PARAGRAM [Wieting et al., 2015] as the specific semantic specialization method used for this process.
Must specify that the final specialized representation used for the word w is the vector v after specialization (not v1 or v2).

Must explain that PARAGRAM is comparable to Retrofitting but includes an automatically generated repelling component, where for each target word to specialize a repelling word is selected either randomly or based on dissimilarity.

decisions: How is the intrinsic evaluation of the proposed method configured in terms of corpus, embedding training setup, and evaluation metric/datasets?

requirements.description: Must state that the intrinsic evaluation uses 1 billion lemmatized words randomly selected from the Annotated English Gigaword corpus [Napoles et al., 2012] at the level of sentences.
Must specify that word embeddings are built using the best parameters reported in Baroni et al. (2014) [Baroni et al., 2014].
Must describe that intrinsic evaluation is based on computing Spearman's rank correlation between human similarity judgments and similarity between word vectors.
Must mention that the Spearman's rank correlation is computed on 3 representative datasets of word pairs.

decisions: How does the paper operationalize synonym extraction for evaluation, including gold standard, retrieval setup, ranking criterion, and IR framing?

requirements.description: Must state that the gold standard for synonym extraction is WordNet synonyms (i.e., synonym sets taken from WordNet).
Must specify that the evaluation is performed only on nouns (i.e., 'evaluated nouns' or 'noun targets' are used as queries).
Must describe that for each evaluated noun, the system retrieves its 100 nearest neighbors in the embedding space.
Must indicate that neighbors are ranked by cosine similarity, from most similar to less similar.
Must characterize the evaluation as an Information Retrieval (IR) paradigm, explicitly mapping the evaluated word to a 'query' and its neighbors to 'documents'.

decisions: How does the paper compute and evaluate sentence similarity using Pseudofit embeddings on the STS Benchmark dataset?

requirements.description: Must state that sentence similarity is evaluated on the Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) Benchmark dataset, explicitly citing it as [Cer et al., 2017].
Must specify that the evaluation metric is Pearson rank correlation between human similarity judgments and the computed similarity between sentences for a set of reference sentence pairs.

Must describe the sentence representation method as a strong baseline approach based on word embeddings, where the sentence vector is obtained by elementwise addition (sum) of the embeddings of the plain words in the sentence.
Must indicate that Pseudofit[max, fus-max-pooling] embeddings are used for this task and that these embeddings are defined specifically for nouns and verbs.
Must state that sentence similarity is computed as the cosine similarity between the resulting sentence representations.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s conclusions about what Pseudofit is, how it works, how it was evaluated, and how it can be extended or related to other embedding methods?

requirements.description: Must state that Pseudofit is a method for improving/specializing word embeddings toward semantic similarity specifically without using any external semantic relations or external knowledge sources, as described in the abstract and conclusion section.

Must describe that the method is based on building several representations (pseudo-senses) for each word from the same corpus and using the convergence of these multiple representations to obtain a more general word representation, as detailed in the method description section.

Must report that Pseudofit was evaluated both intrinsically and extrinsically, and that these evaluations covered at least the three tasks: word similarity, synonym extraction, and sentence similarity, as presented in the experiments/results sections (including any tables summarizing these tasks).
Must capture the paper’s concluding perspective that Pseudofit can be transposed or extended to settings with several corpora, as discussed in the conclusions or future work section.
Must mention that the paper explicitly links Pseudofit to research on meta-embeddings and ensembles of word embeddings, as stated in the discussion or conclusion section on related perspectives.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the example and motivations for text simplification as presented in the paper to generate the 'Text Simplification' slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper defines text simplification (TS) as transforming an original (complex) text into a target (simpler) text, and use this to justify showing a complex–simplified sentence pair on the slide.

Must retrieve from the paper that TS can be targeted to specific audiences (e.g., different school grade levels or non-native speakers) and explicitly reflect this by including a bullet about a specific target audience (e.g., non-native speakers) on the slide.

Must extract that TS is a monolingual text-to-text transformation task distinct from machine translation (MT) but related to it, and represent this relationship by including a bullet that TS can be used for improving NLP tasks such as MT.

Must retrieve and present a concrete example sentence pair from the paper that illustrates TS, where the first sentence is a longer, more complex version and the second is a shorter, simplified version preserving the same meaning (e.g., the amphibian decline example).

Must base the slide content on information from the paper's introductory or problem-definition discussion of text simplification (including its purposes and example transformations), rather than from unrelated sections such as experiments or related work.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of the Newsela corpus and its key properties relevant to audience-targeted text simplification?

requirements.description: Must state that the corpus description explicitly contrasts Wikipedia with Simple Wikipedia (WSW) as a commonly used but less suitable resource for targeted simplification.
Must state that Simple Wikipedia (WSW) is described in the paper as not being professionally simplified.
Must state that Simple Wikipedia (WSW) is described as having no clearly defined target audience.
Must state that, in contrast, the simplified versions in the Newsela corpus are explicitly targeted at different grade levels in the US.
Must state that the paper reports using automatic sentence-level alignments between original and simplified texts in the Newsela corpus.

decisions: How does the paper adapt sequence-to-sequence text simplification models to account for different target audiences or grade levels, and what prior multilingual NMT technique does it build on?

requirements.description: Must state that previous text simplification work generally ignores or disregards the specific needs or specificities of different target audiences (e.g., different grade levels).
Must describe that the proposed approach uses an artificial token prepended to the input sequence to represent the target sentence's grade level or audience in the encoder.
Must identify that the model is a sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) text simplification model, analogous to neural machine translation architectures.
Must reference Google's multilingual NMT approach by Johnson et al. (2017) as the inspiration or basis for using an artificial token to guide the encoder toward a specific target language or style.

Must explain the analogy to Johnson et al. (2017) by indicating that, similar to a language token like '<2es>' used to request Spanish output (e.g., '<2es> How are you?'), the paper uses a grade-level token to request a simplification for a specific grade level.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present how the paper handles text simplification for different grade levels, including example simplifications and robustness to repeated source sentences?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper focuses on producing more adequate text simplifications tailored to different target audiences or grade levels, explicitly linking text simplification outputs to specific grade levels.

Must describe that the grade level (or target audience level) is assumed to be provided by the end-user at inference time, i.e., the model conditions on a user-given grade level rather than inferring it automatically.

Must mention that the approach is designed to be robust to repetitions of the same source sentence, i.e., it can handle multiple occurrences of identical complex sentences without degradation in simplification quality.

Must reproduce or clearly paraphrase the example sentence pair used in the paper to illustrate simplification (the complex sentence about 'dusty handprints' on the fence near Sasabe and its simpler version), preserving the core semantic content of the example.

Must draw from the section of the paper where the authors introduce or motivate audience-specific (grade-level) simplifications, including any illustrative example and discussion of real-world scenarios where the end-user specifies the grade level.

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize coarse-grained sentence-level simplification operations, and how are these operations modeled for prediction at test time?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper defines a set of coarse-grained sentence-level simplification operations used in sentence-level alignments between original and simplified texts.
Must list all four coarse-grained simplification operation labels exactly as defined in the paper: Identical, Elaborate, Split, and Merge.

Must explain that these coarse-grained operations are derived from sentence-level alignments that are available during training but are not available at test time, explicitly mentioning the unavailability of alignment information at test time as a problem.
Must describe that the paper introduces a simplification operations classification component that predicts the four operation types.

Must specify that the classifier used for simplification operations is a four-class Naive Bayes classifier and that it uses nine features (i.e., "four-class classifier Naive Bayes with nine features").

decisions: What neural machine translation (NMT) approach and implementation are used in the experiments and results of the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the core simplification model in the experiments is a neural machine translation (NMT) / sequence-to-sequence approach rather than a rule-based or statistical model.
Must explicitly state that the implementation framework/toolkit used for the NMT approach is OpenNMT, as named in the experimental setup section.

Must retrieve this information specifically from the experiments or implementation details part of the paper (e.g., 'Experiments', 'Experimental Setup', or 'Implementation' subsection), not from the abstract or introduction.
Must clarify that the NMT/OpenNMT setup is used as the default or baseline configuration for the experiments, as described in the paper.

decisions: Which experimental systems and configuration variants are evaluated in the paper’s Experiments and Results section for learning simplifications tailored to specific grade levels?

requirements.description: Must identify that NTS (w2v) is an experimental system used as a baseline and explicitly state that it uses no artificial tokens.
Must identify that the s2s (baseline) model is an experimental system and explicitly state that it uses no artificial tokens.
Must describe the s2s+operation model variant and explicitly distinguish between its predicted (pred) and gold (gold) operation configurations as reported in the Experiments and Results section.

Must describe the s2s+to-grade+operation model variant and explicitly distinguish between its predicted (pred) and gold (gold) operation configurations as reported in the Experiments and Results section.

Must enumerate all model variants jointly compared in the Experiments and Results section, including s2s+to-grade, s2s+operation (pred), s2s+to-grade+operation (pred), s2s+operation (gold), and s2s+to-grade+operation (gold), preserving the pred/gold labeling used in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper illustrate grade-specific text simplifications for different target audiences using a concrete fire safety example?

requirements.description: Must identify that the example demonstrates text simplification tailored to specific school grade levels (Grades 6–5, Grade 4, Grade 3) as distinct target audiences.
Must state that the original complex sentence being simplified is about taking fire safety very seriously and reassuring residents/people about their safety.
Must describe that the example is formatted as multiple lines, each pairing a grade label ("Grades 6-5", "Grade 4", "Grade 3") with a corresponding simplified sentence variant.
Must explain that the example is used to illustrate how the model or approach generates different simplifications of the same source content conditioned on the target grade level.
Must retrieve the specific grade-labeled simplified sentences, including the distinction between "residents" for Grades 6–5 and "people" for Grade 3 in the safety-related sentences.

decisions: How does the paper illustrate zero-shot text simplification between unseen grade-level pairs, specifically from grade level 12 to grade level 4?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper discusses a zero-shot text simplification setting where the model is applied to grade-level pairs that are not present in the training data.
Must state explicitly that the example concerns simplification from grade level 12 (source) to grade level 4 (target).
Must retrieve the detail that there are no training instances for the specific 12-to-4 grade-level pair (i.e., this mapping is unseen in the training set).
Must locate and use the part of the paper where zero-shot or unseen grade-level mappings are introduced or exemplified (e.g., in the experimental setup or results discussion).
Must connect the 12-to-4 example to the broader methodological idea that the model is trained on multiple audience/grade-level simplifications and then evaluated on a new, unseen grade-level pair.

decisions: What main conclusions does the paper draw about using target-audience information and simplification-operation information in text simplification models?

requirements.description: Must state that text simplification (TS) models that do not incorporate explicit target audience or grade-level information produce suboptimal or 'not ideal' results, as concluded in the paper.
Must describe the use of a simple artificial token encoding the grade level (target audience) as an input control signal to the TS model, as presented in the paper's method section.

Must report that conditioning on the grade-level artificial token improves the quality of text simplification and enables target-audience-oriented simplifications, as stated in the conclusions or results discussion.
Must mention that the approach enables zero-shot text simplification for unseen target audiences or grade levels, as explicitly claimed in the conclusions or experimental analysis.

Must identify that the paper uses simplification operation information (e.g., labels or features indicating operations like splitting, deletion, paraphrasing) in a multi-task learning setup to improve a classifier related to the TS task, as described in the methodology or experiments.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s overall goal, specific focus on metaphoric change, and the key methodological components listed in the introduction slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the overall goal of the paper is to build a computational model for detecting semantic change (or semantic change in general), as opposed to only metaphoric change.
Must specify that, within this paper, the particular focus is on distinguishing metaphoric change from other types of semantic change.
Must mention that the method exploits the idea of semantic generality originating from work on hypernym detection (i.e., transferring ideas from hypernym detection).
Must describe that entropy is applied to a distributional semantic model as the core information-theoretic measure used in the approach.
Must identify that the empirical study is conducted on German and that the authors introduce the first diachronic test set/resource for evaluating models of metaphoric change in German.

decisions: What specific shortcomings of prior work on semantic change does the paper identify in contrast to its own focus on metaphoric change?

requirements.description: Must cover the part of the related work / background discussion where the authors enumerate the two main types of prior approaches to semantic change (spatial displacement models and word sense induction models).
Must state that previous work is characterized as focusing on spatial displacement models, explicitly naming them as one of the two main categories of prior approaches.
Must state that previous work is characterized as focusing on word sense induction models, explicitly naming them as the second main category of prior approaches.
Must identify that prior work is criticized for only quantifying the overall degree of semantic change, without being able to qualify or distinguish different types of change.
Must explicitly note that earlier approaches do not examine metaphoric change as a specific type of semantic change.

decisions: What key properties and illustrative examples of metaphoric semantic change does the paper provide that are needed to construct this slide?

requirements.description: Must state that metaphoric change is described as a frequent and important type of semantic change.
Must state that in metaphoric change the source and target concepts are related by similarity (or an explicitly similar phrasing indicating a similarity-based relation).
Must state that metaphoric change often results in more abstract or more general meanings for the affected word.
Must state the assumption that the properties of metaphoric change (i and ii) imply extension and dispersion in the range of linguistic contexts in which the word appears.

Must provide a diachronic lexical example illustrating metaphoric change, including an earlier concrete use (e.g., 'turn around' in a physical sense) and a later abstract/metaphorical use (e.g., 'revolutionize the state').

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the key properties of the Deutsches Textarchiv (erweitert) corpus used in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the main corpus used is the 'Deutsches Textarchiv (erweitert) (DTA)'.
Must state that the DTA corpus contains more than 2,447 lemmatized and POS-tagged texts.
Must report that the DTA corpus comprises more than 140 million tokens.
Must specify that the DTA corpus covers a time period from the late 15th century to the early 20th century.
Must mention that the DTA corpus is balanced by including both literary and scientific texts.

decisions: How does the paper define and interpret the information-theoretic quantity I (word entropy) used to detect metaphoric change?

requirements.description: Must state that I corresponds to the entropy of a word vector (i.e., an information-theoretic entropy measure applied to a target word's distribution over contexts).
Must state that I is assumed to reflect semantic generality in the context of hypernym detection (linking entropy to hypernym-like generality).
Must provide the formal definition of I as an entropy expression over context words ci given a target word w (e.g., I = -∑ P(ci|w) log P(ci|w) or equivalent), not just a verbal description.
Must explicitly define P(ci|w) as the occurrence probability of context word ci given the target word w, matching the paper's notation and conditional relationship.
Must explain that I measures the unpredictability of a target word w's co-occurrences (its distribution over context words), connecting entropy to co-occurrence unpredictability.

decisions: How does the paper construct and annotate its German test set for evaluating metaphoric semantic change?

requirements.description: Must state that there was previously no standard test set for semantic or metaphoric change and that the authors therefore create a new test set.
Must report that the created test set consists of 28 target items (14 changing words plus 14 stable distractors).
Must describe the preselection step where 14 words undergoing metaphoric change are chosen and 14 stable distractor words are added.
Must explain that for each target word the authors identify a specific date (time point) of change and then extract 20 contexts from before and 20 contexts from after this date.
Must describe that contexts from the two time periods are randomly combined into pairs for each word, yielding 560 context pairs in total, which annotators then judge for metaphorical change.

decisions: How does the paper define and operationalize the annotation procedure for identifying metaphoric relations between two contexts (C1 and C2), and what is the resulting annotated resource?

requirements.description: Must state that the annotation task is to identify whether there is a metaphoric relation between two compared contexts or usages labeled C1 and C2.

Must list the four diagnostic criteria used to judge C1 relative to C2: (1) C1 is less concrete than C2, (2) C1 is less human-oriented than C2, (3) C1 is not related to bodily action in contrast to C2, and (4) C1 is less precise than C2.
Must describe the follow-up condition that, if at least one diagnostic criterion holds, annotators check whether C1 contrasts with C2 but can still be understood in comparison with it.
Must report that inter-annotator agreement for this metaphoric relation annotation, measured with Fleiss' Kappa, lies in the range starting at 0.40 (e.g., 'between .40 and ...').
Must state that the outcome of the annotation procedure is a gold ranking of target words according to the strength or degree of metaphoric change.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and present the example from the German metaphoric change test set as shown in Table 1 (sample of test set items ordered by annotated degree of metaphoric change)?

requirements.description: Must state that the example is taken from 'Table 1' and identify it explicitly as a sample of test set items ordered by their annotated degree of metaphoric change.
Must indicate that the items in Table 1 belong to a diachronic test set for German metaphoric change annotation (i.e., they are examples from the metaphoric change test set described in the paper).
Must reproduce or describe the table header fields in the order shown: 'target', 'POS', 'type', 'date', 'meaning', 'score'.
Must correctly retrieve the sample row from Table 1 with the following values: target='thunderstorm', POS='N', type='met', and meaning='thunderstorm, blowup'.

Must reference that this table appears in the part of the paper reporting 'Annotation Results' or equivalent evaluation/annotation section where the test set items and their annotated scores are presented.

decisions: What does Table 2 report about the correlation between the model’s predicted ranks and the gold ranks, and how is statistical significance determined?

requirements.description: Must identify that Table 2 reports a correlation coefficient between predicted ranks and gold (annotated) ranks.
Must explicitly state that the metric in Table 2 is a correlation value (e.g., Pearson or Spearman), not accuracy, F1, or another evaluation metric.
Must state that the statistical significance of the correlation values in Table 2 is assessed using a t-test.
Must reference Table 2 by its label or caption as the source of the correlation between predicted and gold ranks.
Must retrieve the description of the evaluation setup where predicted ranks are compared to gold ranks, as used for the correlations reported in Table 2.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and present the historical German example sentences and their English translations used in the paper’s result analysis of metaphoric change?

requirements.description: Must include the historical German sentence beginning with "Von einem Bawren / welcher einem Kalbskopff die Augen austach." exactly as it appears in the paper’s result analysis examples.
Must include the corresponding English translation "About a Farmer / who cut out the eyes of a calfs head." exactly as it appears paired with the first German example in the paper.

Must include the German sentence "Sie wollen ihre Aufgabe nicht nur losen, sondern auch elegant, d. h. rasch losen, um Nebenbuhler auszustechen." exactly as it appears in the result analysis examples.

Must include the corresponding English translation "They not only wanted to solve their task, but also elegantly, i.e., solve it fast, in order to excel rivals." exactly as it appears paired with the second German example in the paper.

Must include the German sentence "Die Lufft ist hei / vnd gibt viel Blitzen vnd Donnerwetter ..." and its English translation "The air is hot / and there are many lightnings and thunderstorms ..." exactly as they appear together in the result analysis examples.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s main conclusions about using entropy and frequency to detect metaphoric/semantic change and the generalizability of the annotation and model?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper’s conclusions explicitly recommend annotating semantic change in a corpus (i.e., that semantic change can be and should be annotated in corpora).
Must report that entropy correlates strongly and significantly with the degree of metaphoric or semantic change, as concluded in the paper’s results/discussion section.

Must report that word frequency correlates only moderately and not significantly with metaphoric or semantic change, specifically noting that this non-significance is observed on the small dataset used in the study.

Must extract from the conclusion or discussion section that both the annotation scheme and the entropy-based model are generalizable to different types or processes of semantic change beyond metaphoric change in German.
Must identify that the model used to detect metaphoric change is unsupervised and language-independent, as part of the generalizability claim summarized in the conclusions.

decisions: Does the system correctly retrieve and summarize the paper content that motivates emoji ubiquity and cognitive relevance for the introductory slide?

requirements.description: Must state that a cited study found that approximately half of social media text (or posts) contains emojis, matching the "half of social media text contains emojis" claim on the slide.
Must describe that the same parts of the brain are activated when viewing emojis as when viewing a real human face, corresponding to the cognitive/neurological comparison in the slide text.
Must retrieve the fact that Oxford Dictionaries named the "Face With Tears of Joy" emoji as Word of the Year, including the specific emoji name used in the slide.
Must include the Instagram engineering blog URL or its clear reference ("emojineering-part-1-machine-learning-for-emoji" at http://instagram-engineering.tumblr.com/...), as shown on the slide.

Must identify and mention the Churches et al. (2014) study "Emoticons in mind: An event-related potential study" with at least the lead author name (Churches) and the 2014 publication year, as cited on the slide.

decisions: What problem does the paper identify with standard word embeddings and existing resources, and what is the emoji-based goal it proposes for building lexical resources?

requirements.description: Must state that standard word embeddings are described in the paper as not interpretable, specifically in terms of their dimensions or features lacking direct semantic or emotional meaning.
Must explain that standard word embeddings in the paper are said to capture relationships among words only, without explicitly encoding relationships between words and emotions.
Must identify that the paper explicitly notes the absence of an existing lexicon that links emojis to emotions (i.e., a lexicon for emoji–emotion associations does not yet exist).
Must describe the paper's goal of creating interpretable word vectors whose dimensions are based on emotions or emoji-derived emotional features, rather than opaque embedding dimensions.

Must state that the method uses emojis (e.g., from an emoji-centric Twitter corpus) to derive emotion-related features that can be assigned to arbitrary words in text, effectively building an emoji-based lexical resource.

decisions: How did the authors acquire and filter their emoji-centric Twitter dataset, and what metadata fields are stored for each tweet?

requirements.description: Must state that the corpus size is approximately 20 million tweets collected over a period of 1 year, matching the dataset description in the data acquisition section.
Must specify that the collection procedure targeted 100 tweets per day for each of the 620 most frequently used emojis, as described in the dataset construction details.
Must indicate that every tweet in the dataset contains at least one emoji, reflecting the emoji-centric filtering criterion in the data collection methodology.
Must mention the user-level constraint that no more than 5 tweets were collected from any individual user, as stated in the corpus filtering rules.

Must list the tweet-level metadata fields stored for each tweet, including at minimum: tweet-id, text, username, date, retweets, favorites, geo-location, emoji, and hashtags, as defined in the dataset description.

decisions: How does the paper induce vector representations for words and emojis from the tweets corpus and compute their similarity?

requirements.description: Must state that Word2Vec is trained on a tweets (Twitter) corpus, explicitly identifying that the embeddings are learned from tweets rather than another text source.
Must describe that both words and emojis are embedded in the same vector space, i.e., that the model learns vector representations for words and for emojis jointly.
Must explain that similarity between a word vector and an emoji vector is computed using cosine similarity, explicitly naming 'cosine similarity' as the metric.

Must reference or reconstruct the schematic or example that shows a sequence of words (e.g., 'word word2 .. word') and a sequence of emojis (e.g., 'emoji emoji emoji3 emoji620') as inputs to the Word2Vec model, indicating multiple word and emoji tokens.
Must indicate that the purpose of computing cosine similarity between word and emoji vectors is to capture or quantify semantic or emotional association between them.

decisions: How does the EmoTag paper describe its system and problem formulation for the EmoInt WASSA Shared Task on predicting emotion intensity in tweets?

requirements.description: Must state that the task is defined as: given a tweet and an emotion X, determine the intensity or degree of emotion X felt by the speaker.
Must specify that the system predicts the intensity of emotions in tweets as real-valued scores in the continuous range [0,1].
Must list the set of target emotions exactly as: anger, fear, joy, and sadness.
Must identify the main learning approach as a supervised learning method using a Random Forest regressor with exactly 800 trees.

Must describe that the feature set includes the output of a CNN-LSTM network that uses the paper's Emoji Vectors as the word embedding, and that these CNN-LSTM outputs are combined with other features as input to the Random Forest regressor.

decisions: What Pearson correlation results between gold and predicted emotion scores for tweets does the EmoTag paper report for different methods across anger, fear, joy, sadness, and their average, including dimensionality information?

requirements.description: Must identify that the reported metric is the Pearson correlation between gold (ground truth) emotion scores and predicted emotion scores for tweets.
Must retrieve the table that lists Pearson correlation values per method for the four basic emotions (anger, fear, joy, sadness) and an overall average column.
Must extract the column or field labeled 'Methods' that enumerates the different models or baselines whose Pearson correlations are being compared.
Must extract the 'Average' correlation column (or equivalent aggregate performance measure) that summarizes performance across the four emotions for each method.
Must extract the 'Dim' (dimensionality) column or field associated with each method, indicating the representation size or number of dimensions used.

decisions: How does the EmoTag paper generate and evaluate sentiment scores for emojis?

requirements.description: Must state that NRC EmoLex is explicitly used as the lexicon/resource to obtain sentiment or emotion-bearing words associated with emojis in the EmoTag framework.
Must describe the step of selecting the top K words for each emoji based on EmoTag similarity scores, explicitly mentioning that the ranking criterion is the EmoTag similarity score.
Must specify that the final sentiment score for an emoji is computed by aggregating the similarity scores of the top K words, and must explicitly state the value K = 3 as used in the paper.
Must identify that the ground truth for evaluation is taken from the 'Sentiment of Emojis' dataset or study by Novak et al., and must name Novak et al. as the source.

Must draw from the specific part of the paper that describes the sentiment score generation and evaluation procedure for emojis (e.g., the experimental setup or evaluation methodology section), not from unrelated background or data collection sections.

decisions: How does the EmoTag paper evaluate and compare its emoji sentiment scores against Novak’s sentiment scores using Pearson correlation?
