decisions: What are the main contributions, findings, and open questions summarized in the paper’s conclusion slide about learning to rank clarification questions using neural EVPI?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a novel model that integrates deep learning with the classic notion of Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) specifically for ranking clarification questions.

Must report that the authors create a dataset of approximately 77,000 clarification questions (and their answers) with associated context, and a separate evaluation set of size 500 with expert human annotations.
Must describe that the methodology includes explicitly modeling the answer when ranking questions and that this explicit answer modeling helps in identifying good clarification questions.
Must state that the EVPI-based formalism provides an advantage ("leverage") over a similarly expressive feedforward neural network baseline in the task of ranking clarification questions.

Must mention that the paper also explores a sequence-to-sequence based question generation model and raises the open issue of how to automatically evaluate performance, and must include that code and data are released at the GitHub URL: https://github.com/raosudha89/ranking_clarification_questions.

decisions: How does the model apply EVPI-based ranking to clarification question candidates for a specific StackExchange post about excessive disk read/write when launching an application?

requirements.description: Must state that the slide illustrates the model's use of Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) to rank clarification question candidates for a given post.

Must identify that this example comes from the paper's section (or subsection) presenting qualitative/sample outputs or case studies of ranked clarification questions on StackExchange posts, rather than from dataset construction or model training sections.
Must explain that the 'Ranking of Question Candidates EVPI value' column reflects the model's computed EVPI scores used to order the listed clarification questions for the shown StackExchange post.

Must describe that the slide reproduces a concrete example from the paper where the original StackExchange post text (about 'Too much disk read/write when launching an application' on Xubuntu 13.04 on an old Dell Inspiron) is shown above a ranked list of candidate clarification questions.

Must retrieve and list at least the top three ranked clarification question candidates from the example (beginning with 'How much ram do you have installed? and what size is the swap disk partition', followed by 'Can you tell us a little about your configuration ?' and 'What is the longest time you have let it run ?') in the correct order.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s stated motivations and problem statements for inducing à la carte embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that distributed representations (embeddings) for words/text have achieved many successes in NLP tasks, explicitly including at least one of: language modeling, machine translation, or text classification, as described in the paper’s motivation/introduction section.

Must identify the motivation of inducing embeddings for a wide variety of textual features, explicitly mentioning features with very few occurrences such as n-grams or rare words, as framed in the paper’s motivation/introduction discussion.

Must mention that one of the paper’s goals is to develop simple text embeddings using n-gram-based representations that perform well on classification tasks, as stated in the motivation/problem statement portion of the paper.
Must state that another goal is to develop simple unsupervised text embedding methods that can compete with state-of-the-art LSTM-based methods, as described in the motivation/introduction section.

Must convey that the authors claim to make progress on both identified problems (embeddings for rare/feature types such as n-grams, rare words, synsets, and simple competitive unsupervised text embeddings), reflecting the paper’s stated contributions in the introductory or motivation section.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of standard word embedding methods and their core training properties for use as background on word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that the core idea of these word embedding methods is that cooccurring words are trained to have a high inner product (or equivalently, similar vectors for frequently cooccurring words).
Must explicitly identify at least two of the following as example embedding methods: LSA, word2vec, GloVe (or their direct variants), as a group of standard word embedding approaches.
Must describe that these embedding methods are trained on a very large text corpus and require only a small number of passes (epochs) over that corpus.
Must indicate that the training objective for these embedding methods involves non-convex optimization (e.g., non-convex loss or objective function).
Must list at least three downstream NLP tasks for which such word embeddings are used, specifically drawn from: solving analogies, language modeling, machine translation, and text classification.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper motivates and defines the problem of inducing embeddings for rare or unseen non-word textual features (e.g., n-grams, phrases, synsets) and contrasts this with standard word-embedding approaches?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper is concerned with inducing semantic embeddings for non-word textual features such as n-grams, phrases, sentences, annotated words, or synsets, and explicitly mention that these features can have zero or very few occurrences in the corpus.

Must cover the problem motivation section where the authors contrast standard word-embedding-based approaches (e.g., learning embeddings for all features jointly over a corpus) with the need to handle rare or unseen features individually.

Must explain the contrast between a 'prix fixe' approach (learning many parameters and embeddings for all features together at high computational cost) and an 'à la carte' approach (computing embeddings on the fly for specific features), including the claim that standard approaches yield poor quality embeddings for rare features.

Must describe the Firth-inspired assumption that a feature's meaning is derived from the words in its context (i.e., that the method uses surrounding words to infer a feature's embedding from one or a few observed contexts).

Must mention that the paper poses the specific question of whether, given a feature and one or a few contexts of surrounding words, it is possible to efficiently compute a reliable embedding for that feature.

decisions: How does the paper formally define the problem setup for inducing embeddings for new textual features from a corpus with pretrained word embeddings?

requirements.description: Must state that the method assumes access to a text corpus together with high-quality word embeddings that have been pretrained on that same corpus (or on the relevant domain data).
Must identify that the central problem is to induce an embedding for a 'feature' (e.g., rare word, n-gram, synset, or other textual feature) rather than only for standard vocabulary words.

Must describe that the input to the induction procedure is the feature observed in one or more textual contexts (i.e., occurrences of the feature in the corpus, represented via their surrounding words).
Must specify that the desired output is a good-quality embedding vector for the given feature, compatible with the existing pretrained word embedding space.

Must extract the problem setup from the part of the paper that introduces the à la carte embedding task (e.g., the introductory or problem formulation section where inputs and outputs of the method are explicitly defined).

decisions: How does the paper motivate a linear approach for inducing feature embeddings from the contexts of a feature f, particularly regarding stop words and shared components in word vectors?

requirements.description: Must state that the method constructs a representation for a feature f based on the word vectors of words appearing in its context c (e.g., a linear combination or aggregation of context word embeddings).
Must identify that common stop words (e.g., 'is', 'the') are frequent in contexts but are considered less informative for the induced feature embedding.
Must describe that the approach is explicitly linear in the sense that it applies a linear transformation or linear operation to the aggregated context word vectors to obtain the feature embedding.
Must mention that pretrained word vectors tend to share common components (e.g., dominant directions or shared subspace) across many words.

Must explain that, without correction, these shared common components in word vectors would be amplified when aggregating context words, motivating the need for the specific linear treatment or transformation described in the paper.

decisions: What techniques does the paper describe for adjusting word embeddings using SIF weights and the all-but-the-top transformation?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the concept of SIF (Smooth Inverse Frequency) weights as a mechanism to down-weight frequent words in constructing embeddings.

Must retrieve the explicit definition or formula indicating that the SIF weight for a word depends on the frequency of that word in the corpus (i.e., uses the frequency of w in the corpus as an input).
Must state that SIF weighting is analogous or similar to tf-idf in the sense of reducing the influence of very frequent words.
Must identify and describe the 'all-but-the-top' post-processing method, specifically that it removes or subtracts the component of word vectors along the top (dominant) principal direction.

Must locate and use the part of the paper where SIF weighting and all-but-the-top are introduced as preprocessing or post-processing steps for word or feature embeddings (e.g., in a methodology or experimental setup section), not from unrelated background or citations alone.

decisions: How does the paper’s general à la carte embedding approach use matrix operations and unsupervised linear regression over word-based features to learn new feature vectors?

requirements.description: Must state that down-weighting and removing specific directions in the embedding space is implemented via a matrix multiplication (i.e., a learned linear transformation applied to context or feature vectors).

Must describe that the method learns a linear transformation using words as features, where word embeddings (or word co-occurrence–derived representations) serve as the input feature space for inducing new embeddings.
Must explicitly identify that the linear transformation is learned by linear regression (a regression fit from context-based representations to pretrained word vectors or similar targets).
Must state that the learning procedure for the linear transformation is unsupervised, i.e., it does not rely on labeled data but only on distributional statistics or pretrained word vectors.

Must draw these elements (matrix-based down-weighting/removal of directions, word-based features, unsupervised linear regression) from the paper’s method/approach description section rather than from abstract, introduction, or results-only discussion.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the theoretical justification for the linear transformation matrix used in à la carte embeddings, as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that Arora et al. (TACL 2018) prove, under a specific generative model for text, the existence of a matrix that linearly maps context-based features to word embeddings (i.e., a linear transformation relating context vectors to word vectors).
Must describe that this matrix is learned via linear regression using pretrained word vectors and their observed contexts, as specified in the theoretical or methodological part of the paper.

Must report the empirical finding that the learned matrix approximately recovers or reconstructs the original pretrained word vectors from their context representations (i.e., demonstrates good reconstruction quality).

Must draw from the section that provides the theoretical justification or connection to the Arora et al. generative model (e.g., the theory or background section that cites Arora et al. TACL 2018), not from unrelated experimental or application sections.
Must explicitly connect the existence of this matrix under the generative model to the justification for using a single global linear transform in the à la carte embedding method.

decisions: What does the paper identify as the core learned component needed to induce new semantic feature vectors in the à la carte embedding method?

requirements.description: Must state that the à la carte embedding method is centered on learning a single global linear transformation (induction matrix) that maps context-based representations to semantic feature vectors.
Must specify that this induction matrix is learned using linear regression over pretrained word vectors and their associated context representations, as described in the method section.
Must describe that the induction matrix is applied 'on the fly' to derive embeddings for rare or unseen textual features (e.g., rare words, n-grams, synsets) from their observed contexts.
Must reference the part of the paper where the linear transformation or induction matrix is first formally introduced and defined as the main learned parameter of the approach.

decisions: What advantages of the à la carte embedding method does the paper identify compared to standard embedding approaches?

requirements.description: Must state that à la carte embeddings are computed only for a given target feature (e.g., a specific word, n-gram, or synset) rather than for all possible features in the vocabulary.
Must identify that the core optimization step of the à la carte method is a simple linear regression used to learn a linear transformation from context-based representations to embeddings.
Must describe that the computational procedure requires only a single pass over the corpus and feature contexts to gather the necessary statistics for learning the linear transformation.

Must explain that the method is sample efficient in the sense that it learns only a small number of global parameters (those of the linear transformation) instead of separate parameters for every individual feature.
Must state that the method is versatile in that it can induce an embedding for any feature that appears in at least one context in the corpus.

decisions: How does the induction matrix in the à la carte embedding method change word embedding norms across word frequencies compared to the all-but-the-top baseline?

requirements.description: Must identify that the induction matrix (linear transform) is applied to pretrained word embeddings and that its effect is analyzed via changes in embedding norms.
Must reference the specific plot/figure that shows 'Change in Embedding Norm under Transform' as a function of word frequency, comparing the induction matrix to the all-but-the-top method.
Must retrieve from the figure or its caption that the induction matrix mainly down-weights words with very high and very low frequency, while all-but-the-top mainly down-weights frequent words.
Must state that the plotted quantity is the change in the norm of word embeddings before and after applying the induction matrix transform, grouped or binned by word frequency.

Must explicitly contrast the behavior of the induction matrix versus all-but-the-top in terms of which frequency ranges of words are most down-weighted, as reported in the corresponding analysis around the figure.

decisions: How does the paper evaluate the effect of the number of contexts on inducing embeddings for rare words using the CRW dataset, and which baseline methods are used for comparison?

requirements.description: Must identify that the evaluation uses the Contextual Rare Words (CRW) dataset, explicitly noting that it provides contexts for rare words and that it is a subset of the RW dataset from Luong et al. (2013).
Must state the task formulation as predicting human-rated similarity scores for pairs of words using induced embeddings derived from their contexts.
Must specify that evaluation performance is measured using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between the inner product of word embeddings and the human similarity scores.

Must retrieve and list the compared baseline methods exactly as defined in the paper: (1) average of words in context, (2) average of non-stop words, (3) SIF weighted average, and (4) all-but-the-top variants where applicable.

Must identify and cover the specific experimental subsection that analyzes the 'effect of number of contexts' on rare word embedding quality, including its description of the CRW setup and comparison methods (e.g., the subsection describing CRW experiments or rare word similarity evaluation).

decisions: How does the paper define and evaluate the nonce definitional task for inducing embeddings of unseen words or concepts?

requirements.description: Must state that the task is to find or induce an embedding for an unseen word or concept given its textual definition (the 'nonce definitional task').
Must describe the evaluation procedure as ranking the target word or concept by cosine similarity between its induced embedding and its true (pretrained) embedding.
Must retrieve that the example definition used in the paper includes the word 'iodine' with a definition of the form 'is a chemical element with symbol I and atomic number 53'.
Must identify and reference the experimental setup subsection or paragraph that introduces the 'nonce definitional task' and its evaluation metrics (Mean Reciprocal Rank and Median Rank).
Must mention that one baseline method is based on a word2vec average of the definition words with stop words removed, and that this baseline is associated with Herbelot and Baroni (2017).

decisions: How does the paper construct and evaluate n-gram (especially bigram) embeddings using the à la carte method, and what example nearest-neighbor words does it report for specific bigrams?

requirements.description: Must state that n-gram (including bigram) embeddings are induced from their contexts in a text corpus, rather than being trained as standalone tokens.
Must describe that the quality of a bigram embedding is evaluated by computing its nearest neighbor words using cosine similarity in the embedding space.

Must retrieve and list the example nearest-neighbor words for the bigram 'beef up' (e.g., 'cutting edge', 'tight lipped', 'meat, out', 'cut, edges', 'loose, fitting') as reported in the paper (typically from a table or example list).

Must retrieve and list the example nearest-neighbor words for the bigram 'but' (contrastive conjunction bigram example) such as 'however', 'which, both', 'which, but', 'but, however' as reported in the paper (typically from a table or example list).

Must retrieve and list at least two additional example bigrams and their nearest-neighbor words (e.g., 'add, reallocate', 'science, multidisciplinary', 'naruto, pokemon', 'a la carte') as shown in the paper's n-gram embedding examples table or figure.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize how the paper’s unsupervised text embedding method works and how its performance compares to baselines such as bag-of-ngrams and LSTMs?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper’s embeddings are learned in an unsupervised way by predicting surrounding words or textual context (e.g., neighboring words or sentences), rather than using labeled supervision.

Must describe that text representations for larger units (e.g., sentences like "This movie is great!") are constructed as a sum or simple composition (e.g., additive combination) of word or n-gram embeddings, as specified in the method section.

Must state that the proposed embedding approach achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or competitive performance on at least some evaluated tasks, as explicitly reported in the experimental results section.
Must retrieve from the results tables or quantitative evaluation that the proposed method matches or outperforms bag-of-ngrams baselines on at least one benchmark task.
Must retrieve from the results tables or quantitative evaluation that the proposed method matches or is competitive with LSTM-based models on at least one benchmark task.

decisions: What does the paper present about linear schemes for n-gram embeddings and the comparative evaluation table of different n-gram embedding methods and their performance on multiple text classification benchmarks?

requirements.description: Must state that in the paper, linear schemes for text representation are described as (or assumed to be) weighted sums of n-gram embeddings, using wording equivalent to 'linear schemes are typically weighted sums of ngram embeddings'.
Must identify that the paper explicitly distinguishes or lists different 'types of n-gram embeddings' (e.g., different methods or variants for constructing n-gram vectors) as a conceptual category.

Must retrieve from the paper a table that has a 'Method' column and an 'n' (or n-gram size) column together with a 'dimension' column, indicating for each method the n-gram order and embedding dimensionality.

Must retrieve from the same table the benchmark dataset column headers: MR, CR, SUBJ, MPQA, TREC, SST (or SST-1), SST (1) (or equivalent single-sentence SST variant), and IMDB, as performance columns associated with each method.

Must recognize that the table reports comparative performance results of multiple n-gram embedding methods across the listed datasets (MR, CR, SUBJ, MPQA, TREC, SST, IMDB), not just listing dataset names without indicating that they are evaluation metrics.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the main conclusions and resources of the à la carte embedding paper as presented in the Conclusions slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper proposes a simple and efficient method for inducing embeddings for many kinds of features (e.g., rare words, n-grams, synsets) given at least one context of usage, as described in the conclusions or main method summary.
Must state that the induced embeddings lie in the same semantic space as standard word embeddings, explicitly noting this compatibility as a conclusion of the paper.

Must report that the method shows good empirical performance specifically for rare words, n-grams, and synsets, matching the performance claims made in the experimental results or conclusion sections.
Must state that the induced text embeddings perform competitively with unsupervised LSTM-based models, reflecting the comparative performance claim made in the results or conclusion sections.

Must identify that the authors provide two external resources: (1) the implementation code hosted on GitHub at a URL matching https://github.com/NLPrinceton/ALaCarte, and (2) the CRW dataset hosted at a URL matching http://nlp.cs.princeton.edu/CRW/.

decisions: What future research directions do the authors propose for extending the à la carte embedding method?

requirements.description: Must identify and state the future work item that concerns zero-shot learning of feature embeddings, using the explicit phrase "zero shot" or "zero-shot" in connection with feature embeddings.
Must identify and state the future work item that focuses on harder-to-annotate features, explicitly mentioning "features" and "synsets" together as an example of such features.
Must identify and state the future work item that proposes using contexts based on alternative syntactic structures, explicitly mentioning "contexts" and "syntactic" (or "syntactic structures").

Must retrieve these three items specifically from the paper's discussion of limitations or future work (e.g., conclusion or future work section), not infer them from the abstract or experimental sections.

Must present the three future work items as distinct bullet-like points or clearly separated ideas, each corresponding to: (1) zero-shot feature embeddings, (2) harder-to-annotate features such as synsets, and (3) contexts based on other syntactic structures.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the basic definition and example of semantic parsing as introduced in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that semantic parsing is about mapping natural language utterances to structured meaning or structured representations, using wording equivalent to 'mapping natural language to structured representations'.
Must explicitly mention that the example utterance is a natural language query about flights (e.g., an utterance like 'all flights from dallas before 10am').
Must retrieve and use the specific example utterance 'all flights from dallas before 10am' (or a trivially equivalent casing/punctuation variant) as the illustrative example of semantic parsing.
Must identify that the example comes from the ATIS dataset and explicitly reference it by name ('ATIS').
Must attribute the ATIS example to Kwiatkowski et al., 2011, including both the author surname 'Kwiatkowski' and the year '2011'.

decisions: What prior neural semantic parsing architectures and high-level encoder-decoder structure does the paper identify when motivating its coarse-to-fine decoding approach?

requirements.description: Must identify and distinguish between a 'sequence decoder' and a 'syntactically-constrained decoder' as two classes of neural semantic parsing architectures discussed in the paper.
Must attribute the 'sequence decoder' approach specifically to prior work by Jia and Liang (2016), Dong and Lapata (2016), and Ling et al., as cited in the paper.
Must attribute the 'syntactically-constrained decoder' approach specifically to prior work by Dong and Lapata (2016), as cited in the paper.
Must describe the high-level architecture diagram that includes the labeled components 'Input Utterance', 'Structured Representation', 'Encoder', and 'Decoder', in that encoder-decoder flow order.

Must state that these prior decoders (sequence and syntactically-constrained) are characterized in the paper as not requiring an explicit manually-designed grammar or logical form schema, corresponding to the slide fragment 'do not require a ...'.

decisions: How does the paper illustrate the idea of glossing over low-level details such as arguments and variable names in the coarse sketch stage of semantic parsing?

requirements.description: Must state that the model decomposes semantic parsing into two stages, where the first stage produces a coarse sketch that omits low-level details like variable names and arguments, as described in the abstract.

Must explicitly mention that low-level information such as arguments and variable names is intentionally glossed over or left unspecified in the initial sketch representation, using wording consistent with the abstract phrase "low-level information (such as variable names and arguments) is glossed over."

Must describe that the second stage of the proposed architecture fills in the missing low-level details (e.g., arguments and variable names) by conditioning on both the natural language input and the previously generated sketch, as stated in the abstract.

Must connect the example utterance "all flights from dallas before 10am" to the notion of a meaning representation where specific arguments (such as city names and time constraints) would be treated as low-level details to be filled in after the coarse sketch.

Must extract the explanation of the coarse-to-fine decomposition directly from the problem/approach description in the abstract or corresponding introductory description, not infer it solely from experimental results or unrelated sections.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s coarse meaning sketch concept, including its illustrative examples and stated advantages, as presented on the 'Meaning Sketch' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that the model uses a coarse-to-fine (sketch then details) semantic parsing approach that explicitly disentangles high-level from low-level semantics, using wording equivalent to "Disentangle high-level from low-level semantics" and "Model meaning at different levels of granularity" from the paper.

Must describe the notion of a "meaning sketch" as a more compact, coarse representation that omits low-level details (e.g., variable names, arguments), using language equivalent to "More compact meaning representation" and "Explicit sharing coarse structure" as motivations or properties.

Must cover the part of the paper where the authors explain how the coarse sketch provides global context to the fine-grained decoder, using phrasing equivalent to "Provide global context to fine meaning decoder" and "Know what the basic meaning of input looks like."

Must mention that the coarse sketch enables sharing of common structure across examples with the same basic meaning, using wording equivalent to "Explicit sharing coarse structure" and "For examples that have the same basic meaning."

Must retrieve and describe at least one code-like or query-like example used in the paper to illustrate the meaning sketch (e.g., an if-statement pattern like "if len(NAME) < NUMBER or NAME[NUMBER] != STRING:" or a SQL-style query like "SELECT Record Company WHERE (Year of Recording AND (Conductor Mikhail Snitko))"), including both the natural language question and its corresponding structured representation at the sketch level.

decisions: How does the coarse-to-fine semantic parser use a sketch to constrain decoding in the method, as illustrated by the example where one argument is missing and type information is shown?

requirements.description: Must state that the method decomposes decoding into two stages: first generating a rough sketch of the meaning representation (omitting low-level details like arguments), then filling in missing details conditioned on both the natural language input and the sketch.

Must describe that the sketch-guided decoding stage uses the sketch to constrain the output space of the decoder, i.e., the decoder is restricted to produce structures consistent with the previously generated sketch.

Must reference the example figure in the method section that shows the input utterance "all flights before 10" (or equivalent) being encoded and mapped to a lambda-calculus style logical form containing 'flight', 'departure', and a time argument, with an intermediate sketch where at least one argument position is left unspecified (e.g., marked with a placeholder like '?').

Must identify that the example figure explicitly illustrates two cases labeled along the lines of "Example 1: one argument is missing" and "Example 2: type information" to demonstrate how the sketch omits an argument and/or encodes type constraints.

Must draw from the method/approach section that explains 'Input Encoding' and 'Sketch-Guided' decoding, including mention that the natural language input is first encoded and then used together with the sketch in the second-stage decoder.

decisions: How does the proposed coarse-to-fine semantic parser define its training objective and the role of input, sketch, and full meaning representation during training and inference?

requirements.description: Must identify that the model decomposes decoding into two stages: first generating a coarse sketch of the meaning representation, then filling in low-level details to obtain the full meaning representation.

Must state that the training objective is to maximize the log likelihood of the correct structured meaning representation (or equivalently, the joint/conditional likelihood over sketch and full meaning representation given the input utterance).

Must explicitly map the three variables used in the slide to the paper's notation or description: (1) the natural language input utterance, (2) the intermediate sketch representation, and (3) the final detailed meaning representation.
Must draw from the paper's training or learning section (where the log-likelihood objective is defined) rather than from experimental results, related work, or introduction sections.
Must indicate that the sketch omits low-level information such as variable names and arguments, as described in the paper, distinguishing it from the full meaning representation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and present the three example neural semantic parsing tasks and their illustrative utterances/queries as shown on the 'Neural Semantic Parsing Tasks' slide?

requirements.description: Must state that one task is 'Natural language to logical form' and explicitly associate it with the Geo/ATIS datasets as shown on the slide.
Must state that one task is 'Natural language to source code' and explicitly associate it with the Django dataset as shown on the slide.
Must state that one task is 'Natural language to SQL' and explicitly associate it with the WikiSQL dataset as shown on the slide.
Must reproduce or closely paraphrase the example logical-form question: 'what is the population of the state with the largest area?' under the Geo/ATIS logical form task.

Must reproduce or closely paraphrase the example SQL question and partial query for WikiSQL, including the natural language question about 'conductor Mikhail Snitko' and the SQL fragment 'SELECT Record Company WHERE (Year of Recording AND'.

decisions: How does the paper define and handle the arguments of a predicate or operator when mapping natural language utterances to logical forms in its coarse-to-fine semantic parsing framework?

requirements.description: Must identify that in the proposed semantic parsing framework, arguments correspond to the low-level details (such as variable names and argument values) that are intentionally glossed over in the initial coarse sketch of the meaning representation.

Must state that the model decomposes decoding into two stages where the first stage predicts a sketch specifying predicates/operators and their argument slots, and the second stage fills in these argument slots using the natural language input and the sketch.

Must explicitly distinguish between predicates/operators and their arguments in the logical form, indicating that predicates/operators define the structure while arguments provide specific entities, variables, or values.

Must draw from the part of the paper that formally describes the meaning representation or logical form (e.g., the section where the authors define predicates/operators and their arguments in the target formalism), not solely from the abstract.

Must reference at least one concrete example or figure (if present in the paper) that illustrates a logical form where a predicate or operator is shown together with its arguments, and use this to ground the notion of 'arguments of predicate or operator'.

decisions: How does the paper describe handling built-in keywords when mapping natural language utterances to source-code-like meaning representations?

requirements.description: Must state that the approach involves substituting concrete code tokens with their corresponding token types (e.g., abstracting away specific identifiers or literals into type-level placeholders).
Must describe that built-in keywords in the target representation (such as language keywords or boolean constants) are treated specially as fixed token types rather than as arbitrary variable names.
Must retrieve at least one explicit example of a built-in keyword from the paper (e.g., 'True', 'while', or similar) used to illustrate the substitution into token types.

Must draw this information from the part of the paper that explains preprocessing or representation of target programs/meaning representations (e.g., the section describing how utterances are mapped to code-like structures or sketches).

Must connect the token-type substitution to the paper's coarse-to-fine or sketch-based representation idea, indicating that low-level details like specific tokens are abstracted away in the coarse representation.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and extract the paper’s coarse-to-fine sketch-based SQL generation components and their illustration for question-to-table semantic parsing needed to build this slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the model uses a coarse-to-fine (sketch-then-detail) decoding strategy for semantic parsing, where an initial high-level sketch of the SQL query structure (e.g., SELECT, WHERE, aggregation, logical operators) is generated before filling in specific columns and values.

Must describe the figure or diagram in the paper that illustrates question-to-table attention, specifically showing an input natural language question aligned with table columns (e.g., a layout with 'Input Question' and at least two 'Column' fields side by side).

Must explain the sketch classification component that predicts structural elements of the SQL WHERE clause, including logical operators such as AND and comparison operators like '>' and '=' before slot-filling specific column names and values.

Must retrieve and describe the mechanism that points to table columns and text spans (a pointer or attention-based module) used to fill in cond_column and cond_value slots in the SQL sketch from the question and table schema.

Must identify that the model supports SQL aggregation operations (e.g., MIN, MAX, SUM, AVG, COUNT) as part of the sketch for SELECT clauses, which are later instantiated with specific column names such as 'President' or 'Number of Presidents'.

decisions: Which baseline and proposed models are compared in the experimental results section for semantic parsing performance?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'Coarse2Fine' is the proposed model name introduced in this paper and appears as a distinct system in the experimental comparisons.
Must retrieve from the experimental results section the full list of model names that appear together in the comparison: 'Seq2Seq', 'Seq2Tree', 'ASN', 'OneStage', and 'Coarse2Fine'.

Must locate and use the part of the paper where experimental baselines are listed (typically in the 'Experiments' or 'Experimental Results' section) as the source for the model names shown on the slide.
Must recognize and extract that 'Aug Pointer Network (Zhong et al., 2017)' is cited as a specific baseline method used for comparison in the experiments.

Must preserve the grouping of all compared systems (Seq2Seq, Seq2Tree, ASN, OneStage, Coarse2Fine, Aug Pointer Network (Zhong et al., 2017)) as they co-occur in the same table or figure summarizing experimental results, without adding or omitting model names.

decisions: How does the paper present and compare sketch prediction accuracy across the Geo, ATIS, Django, and WikiSQL datasets?

requirements.description: Must identify that 'sketch accuracy' refers specifically to the accuracy of predicting the high-level meaning representation sketch (without low-level details) in the proposed coarse-to-fine semantic parsing framework.
Must retrieve the table or quantitative results section where sketch accuracy is reported separately from full parsing accuracy for multiple datasets, including Geo, ATIS, Django, and WikiSQL.
Must use content from the experimental results section that explicitly evaluates the sketch prediction stage (first-stage decoder) rather than overall end-to-end parsing performance.
Must extract and align the sketch accuracy metrics for all four datasets (Geo, ATIS, Django, WikiSQL) in a way that supports a side-by-side comparison on a single slide.

Must reflect the grouping of the four datasets (Geo, ATIS, Django, WikiSQL) as column or axis labels in a figure or table that specifically visualizes sketch accuracy, not other metrics such as exact match or denotation accuracy.

decisions: How does the paper evaluate the performance of the Coarse2Fine model when provided with an oracle meaning sketch across the Geo, ATIS, Django, and WikiSQL datasets?

requirements.description: Must identify and describe the concept of an 'oracle sketch' (or 'oracle meaning sketch') as used in the paper, i.e., a setting where the gold/ground-truth sketch is given to the decoder instead of a predicted sketch.

Must locate and use the specific section or subsection where the authors report results for 'Coarse2Fine + Oracle Sketch' (often in an ablation or analysis section distinct from the main test accuracy table).

Must retrieve the performance numbers (e.g., accuracy or exact match) for the 'Coarse2Fine + Oracle Sketch' setting for all four datasets: Geo, ATIS, Django, and WikiSQL, from the relevant table or experimental results text.
Must correctly associate each dataset name (Geo, ATIS, Django, WikiSQL) with its corresponding 'Coarse2Fine + Oracle Sketch' result values, without mixing metrics or datasets.

Must explicitly distinguish the 'Coarse2Fine + Oracle Sketch' results from the standard Coarse2Fine model results (without oracle), indicating that these are oracle-based upper-bound or diagnostic results rather than the main test setting.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s proposed directions for future work related to meaning sketches and their annotation?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper introduces and uses the concept of a 'meaning sketch' (or 'sketch of meaning representation') as a central abstraction in its semantic parsing approach, and ground all future work items in this concept.

Must extract content specifically from the paper’s Future Work or Conclusion-style discussion section where limitations and extensions of meaning sketches are described, rather than from methodology or experiments sections.
Must state that one future direction is exploring alternative ways of defining meaning sketches, i.e., varying how the rough sketch of the meaning representation is specified or formalized.

Must state that another future direction is investigating different levels of granularity for meaning sketches, explicitly referring to coarser vs. finer sketch representations of the meaning structure.

Must report that the authors propose, as future work, using meaning sketches to reduce the search space and potentially annotating only meaning sketches (rather than full meaning representations) for some training examples, capturing both the search-space reduction and partial-annotation ideas.

decisions: How does the exemplar encoder-decoder model encode conversational context and define its training objective for generating novel responses?

requirements.description: Must state that the model uses a context encoder based on a recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture to encode the dialogue context.
Must specify that the context encoder is hierarchical (i.e., operates at multiple levels such as utterance-level and conversation-level) rather than a single flat RNN.

Must describe the training objective as maximizing the log probability of the ground-truth (GT) response given the encoded context (i.e., a conditional log-likelihood objective p(response | context)).
Must explicitly indicate that the model is generative in the sense that it can produce novel responses for novel contexts, not limited to copying retrieved responses.
Must draw these details (hierarchical RNN context encoder and log-probability objective) from the model architecture / training objective description section, not from the abstract or related work.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and summarize the paper’s description of retrieval-based conversation models and their limitations that motivate using generative models?

requirements.description: Must state that in the baseline retrieval approach, a response is selected from training data using a nearest-neighbor style index (e.g., TF-IDF or similar similarity search over context-response pairs).
Must explicitly describe that retrieval-based conversation models are particularly suited to closed-domain settings, where all or most valid answers are present in the training corpus.
Must explain that retrieved responses are grounded in the original training domain (i.e., they come directly from domain-specific training conversations, ensuring domain-appropriate answers).
Must mention that retrieval-based systems allow easy filtering or pruning of candidate responses according to external requirements or constraints before selecting the final answer.

Must clearly state the key limitation that pure retrieval models cannot generate novel responses beyond those seen in the training data, motivating the use of generative models to address this limitation.

decisions: How does the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder model retrieve and use exemplar conversations for a given input context?

requirements.description: Must state that an index is built offline from all training context-response pairs, explicitly mentioning both 'context' and 'response' in the description of the indexed items.
Must describe that for each input context c, the system retrieves a set (multiple items) of exemplar contexts together with their corresponding responses from the index.
Must explain that exemplar contexts are matched with the current input context c to compute similarity scores between each exemplar context and c.

Must specify that the similarity scores between the input context and exemplar contexts are used as weights applied to the corresponding exemplar responses (i.e., responses are weighted by these similarities).

Must reference or reconstruct the pipeline-style flow shown in the slide (Input Context → Index → Exemplar conversations), indicating a sequential process from input context through index lookup to retrieved exemplar conversations.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify how the EED model matches exemplar contexts and uses normalized similarities to weight exemplar responses when generating replies?

requirements.description: Must state that the model retrieves similar conversation examples as context–response pairs from the training data and treats them as exemplars for the current input context.

Must explain that similarity is computed between the input context and the contexts of retrieved exemplar context–response pairs, and that these similarity scores are then normalized (e.g., to sum to 1) to obtain weights.

Must describe that the normalized similarity weights are applied specifically to the retrieved exemplar responses (not the contexts) to form exemplar vectors that condition or guide the decoder during response generation.

Must cover the part of the paper that details the exemplar matching and weighting mechanism (e.g., the subsection that defines how exemplar contexts are matched and how their contributions are combined), rather than only the high-level model description or retrieval step.

Must explicitly mention that the contribution of each retrieved response to the final generated response is proportional to the similarity between its associated context and the current input context, reflecting the "contribution is weighed by similarity" idea from the abstract or method section.

decisions: How does the paper conceptually treat exemplar contexts and responses within the objective formulation of the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder model?

requirements.description: Must state that the model treats exemplar contexts and exemplar responses as latent variables in its conceptual or mathematical formulation of the objective.
Must identify that these latent variables correspond specifically to the retrieved exemplar context-response pairs used by the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder, not arbitrary hidden states.

Must draw this latent-variable interpretation from the part of the paper where the training or optimization objective of the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder is defined or analyzed (e.g., the objective or model formulation subsection), rather than from the abstract or introduction alone.

Must connect the latent-variable view to the role of exemplar information in response generation, i.e., that the decoder conditions on or is influenced by these exemplar latent variables when generating the output response.

Must distinguish between observed input context and retrieved exemplars by explicitly indicating that the input context is observed data while exemplar contexts/responses are treated as latent variables within the objective or probabilistic view.

decisions: How does the paper evaluate the Exemplar Encoder-Decoder model, specifically in terms of retrieval method, dataset, and evaluation metrics?

requirements.description: Must state that a TF-IDF based retrieval model is used to retrieve similar exemplar conversations (context-response pairs) from the training data for evaluation.
Must identify the IBM Tech Support dataset as one of the datasets used in the experimental evaluation of the model.
Must describe that retrieved responses are used to construct exemplar vectors which are then utilized by the decoder during response generation.
Must mention that the evaluation includes Activity and Entity based metrics (or similarly named metrics) as part of the quantitative assessment of generated responses.

Must extract these elements (TF-IDF retrieval, IBM Tech Support dataset, Activity and Entity metrics) from the paper's experimental or evaluation section rather than from the abstract alone, if such a section exists.

decisions: Does the summary correctly describe how the paper defines and reports Activity and Entity metrics, including their F1 scores for the retrieval-only model?

requirements.description: Must state that Activity and Entity metrics are defined by comparing specific nouns and verbs (or activity/entity tokens) in the generated response against those in the ground-truth response.
Must explicitly mention that precision, recall, and F1 score are computed for these Activity and Entity metrics when comparing generated responses to ground-truth responses.
Must identify and draw from the evaluation or experiments section where Activity and Entity metrics are introduced and formally defined as part of the evaluation protocol.
Must retrieve and report the Activity F1 score value for the retrieval-only model from the relevant results table or text passage that lists metric scores for different models.
Must retrieve and report the Entity F1 score value for the retrieval-only model from the same results table or text passage that provides metric scores for different models.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the embedding-based automatic evaluation metrics and their (lack of) correlation with human judgments on the Ubuntu dataset, as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that the embedding-based metrics evaluate responses by comparing word embeddings of the generated response with the words (or word embeddings) of the ground-truth response.
Must explicitly reference or clearly derive content from the paper's evaluation or metrics section where embedding-based automatic metrics are defined or discussed.
Must state that these embedding-based metrics do not correlate (or correlate poorly) with human judgments on the Ubuntu dialogue dataset.
Must identify that the empirical finding about lack of correlation with human judgments is based on experiments conducted on the Ubuntu dataset (or Ubuntu dialogue corpus).

Must attribute or connect the discussion of embedding-based metrics and their limitations to prior work, specifically the study titled 'How NOT To Evaluate Your Dialogue System: An Empirical Study of Unsupervised Evaluation Metrics for Dialogue Response Generation' or an equivalent citation.

decisions: Does the summary correctly capture the paper’s discussion about how the exemplar-based generative model uses similar conversations, its ability to generate grounded novel responses, the empirical performance gains from incorporating retrieved conversations, and the generality of the approach to other tasks like image captioning and neural machine translation?

requirements.description: Must state that the proposed model is a generative conversation model that explicitly utilizes retrieved similar conversations (context–response pairs) from the training data for response generation, as described in the main model description section.

Must explain that retrieved conversations are incorporated during generation via exemplar vectors derived from retrieved responses, whose contributions are weighted by the similarity between the retrieved contexts and the current input context, as specified in the model architecture section.

Must report that incorporating retrieved conversations during generation improves performance over baselines, explicitly referencing at least one quantitative metric (e.g., BLEU, perplexity, or other reported scores) from the experimental results tables or figures to support this claim.

Must state that the model can generate novel responses (i.e., not simple copies of retrieved responses) while remaining grounded in the domain of the training data, as discussed in the analysis or discussion of generation behavior.

Must mention that the proposed exemplar-based idea is claimed to be generalizable beyond dialogue to at least image captioning and neural machine translation, as stated in the discussion or conclusion section.

decisions: What are the dataset-related contributions of the paper that should appear on the 'Paper Contributions' slide under the 'Dataset' heading?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a new noun phrase-annotated SMS corpus based on the NUS SMS Corpus.
Must report that the new corpus contains 76,490 noun phrases annotated from 26,500 SMS messages, as specified in the abstract or dataset description.
Must identify and use the section (or subsection) describing the construction/annotation of the new SMS noun phrase corpus, rather than sections on models or experiments.
Must indicate that the annotations were performed by university students, as described in the corpus annotation details.
Must retrieve and include the citation information that the corpus is based on the NUS SMS Corpus by Tao Chen and Min-Yen Kan (2013), as referenced in the paper.

decisions: How did the authors create the NP-annotated SMS corpus, specifically in terms of the annotation tool and annotator population used?

requirements.description: Must state that noun phrases (NPs) in the SMS corpus were manually annotated rather than automatically derived.
Must explicitly identify the annotation tool as the Brat Rapid Annotation Tool (BRAT), matching the name used in the paper.
Must specify that the annotators were undergraduate or university students, as described in the corpus creation process.
Must draw the annotation details (tool and annotator type) from the corpus construction/annotation methodology section rather than from model or experiment sections.
Must connect the annotation process (tool and annotators) specifically to noun phrase annotation in the NUS SMS Corpus, not to any other linguistic unit or corpus.

decisions: What are the main high-level components (Contributions, Models, Experiments, Conclusion) that structure the paper’s content and should appear as section headers on the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly presents a distinct section describing its main contributions (often labeled 'Contributions' or equivalent) and map this to the 'Contributions' item on the slide.
Must identify that the paper contains a section detailing the graphical models used (e.g., semi-Markov CRFs and the novel variant) and map this to the 'Models' item on the slide.

Must identify that the paper includes an empirical evaluation or experiments section (e.g., describing accuracy and running time comparisons on the new dataset) and map this to the 'Experiments' item on the slide.

Must identify that the paper has a concluding section summarizing findings (e.g., similar accuracy but significantly lower running time for the new semi-CRF variant) and map this to the 'Conclusion' item on the slide.

Must recognize that the four slide items 'Contributions', 'Models', 'Experiments', and 'Conclusion' are top-level structural elements of the paper and not subpoints of annotation statistics or other content.

decisions: What notation and label scheme does the paper use to describe sequence length, label set size, maximum segment length, and NP chunk tags when comparing models?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper defines n explicitly as the number of words in a sentence ("n : # words in the sentence").
Must state that the paper defines |Y| explicitly as the number of labels ("|Y| : # labels").
Must state that the paper defines L explicitly as the maximum segment length ("L : max segment length").
Must describe a figure or schematic in the paper that shows three aligned label rows using the tags B, N, and O across multiple token positions (e.g., "B B B N N N" / "N N N N N N" / "O O O O O O").
Must explain that B, N, and O are the NP chunk label types used in the model comparison (e.g., B for beginning of NP, N for inside/continuation of NP, O for outside).

decisions: What empirical components (contributions, dataset, models, and conclusion) does the paper present and verify in its experiments?

requirements.description: Must identify that one core empirical contribution is the introduction of a new annotated corpus of noun phrases derived from the NUS SMS Corpus (informal text SMS messages).
Must state the key dataset statistics used in the empirical verification: 76,490 noun phrases annotated from 26,500 SMS messages.
Must describe that the empirical study compares several graphical models for noun phrase chunking, including a conventional semi-Markov CRF (semi-CRF) and a novel variant of semi-CRF.
Must report that empirically the new semi-CRF variant achieves similar accuracy to the conventional semi-CRF on the new dataset.
Must report that empirically the new semi-CRF variant has significantly lower running time than the conventional semi-CRF on the new dataset.

decisions: How does the paper structure and compare the different CRF-based models and feature configurations whose F1 scores are reported?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper compares three distinct sequence labeling models for NP chunking: a Linear CRF, a standard Semi-CRF, and a novel Weak Semi-CRF, using exactly these model names or their clearly defined equivalents from the model description section.

Must retrieve from the methodology/experiments section that the feature sets are organized into at least two configurations, explicitly including a 'basic features' configuration and an extended configuration that adds affix-based features (e.g., '+affixes').

Must locate the table or experimental results subsection that reports F1 scores for the three models (Linear CRF, Semi-CRF, Weak Semi-CRF) under different feature configurations, and extract the model–feature configuration grid structure (rows/columns) used for comparison.

Must use information from the experimental setup/results section that explicitly ties the F1 score evaluation to the NUS SMS-based NP chunking dataset introduced in the paper, rather than any external or generic dataset.

Must reflect the comparative layout used in the paper (e.g., a table or figure) where models (Linear CRF, Semi-CRF, Weak Semi-CRF) are juxtaposed against feature configurations (basic features, +affixes, all features), preserving this two-dimensional comparison structure in the slide content.

decisions: How does the average training time per iteration scale with the number of SMS training instances for the different models evaluated in the paper?

requirements.description: Must identify that the comparison concerns training speed (average time per training iteration) across the graphical models evaluated for NP chunking, including the novel weak semi-Markov CRF variant and the conventional semi-CRF baseline.

Must retrieve and describe the specific figure or plot (if present) that shows 'Avg. time per iteration' as a function of the number of training instances (SMS), including the axes semantics (x-axis: # training instances/SMS; y-axis: average time per iteration in seconds).

Must extract the numerical values or curves from the paper that report average time per iteration (in seconds) for at least two models (including the novel semi-CRF variant and the conventional semi-CRF) at one or more training set sizes (number of SMS messages).

Must identify from the experimental setup section how training time per iteration was measured (e.g., hardware, implementation, or training configuration) to ensure the timing comparison between models is directly comparable.

Must state the empirical finding that the new semi-CRF variant achieves significantly lower training time per iteration than the conventional semi-CRF while maintaining similar accuracy, explicitly linking this result to the timing data or figure used for the slide.

decisions: Does the summary correctly state the paper’s main contributions regarding the new NP-annotated informal text dataset and the efficiency–accuracy tradeoff of the proposed semi-CRF variant for NP chunking?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper introduces a new noun phrase (NP) annotated corpus/dataset derived from the NUS SMS Corpus (informal text/SMS messages).
Must mention that the new corpus contains NP annotations on informal text messages, specifically referencing that it is based on 26,500 SMS messages (even if the exact NP count is omitted).
Must describe that the model contribution involves a variant of semi-Markov CRFs (semi-CRF) where the decisions of selecting segment length and segment type are split or decoupled.
Must state that the proposed semi-CRF variant achieves similar or comparable accuracy to the conventional semi-CRF on the new dataset.
Must state that the proposed semi-CRF variant has significantly lower or improved running/training time compared to the conventional semi-CRF.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe the three core VAD dimensions of word meaning and illustrate them with appropriate comparative word examples as presented in the paper?

requirements.description: Must state that valence, arousal, and dominance are three primary, largely independent dimensions of word meaning as established in prior factor analysis studies.
Must define valence specifically in terms of a continuum from positive/pleasure to negative/displeasure, matching the polarity described in the paper.
Must define arousal specifically in terms of a continuum from active/stimulated to sluggish/bored, matching the descriptors used in the paper.
Must define dominance specifically in terms of a continuum from powerful/strong to powerless/weak, matching the descriptors used in the paper.

Must retrieve and use the specific comparative word examples from the paper that illustrate each dimension: 'banquet' vs. 'funeral' for valence, 'nervous' vs. 'lazy' for arousal, and 'queen' vs. 'delicate' for dominance.

decisions: How does the paper motivate the need for human annotations of words for valence, arousal, and dominance (VAD), and what applications of such annotations does it identify?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper involves human annotations (human ratings) of words specifically for the three affective dimensions: valence, arousal, and dominance (VAD).

Must extract from the motivation/introduction portion of the paper the use of VAD word annotations by automatic systems for predicting VAD of words and for predicting sentiment and emotions of larger text units such as sentences or tweets.
Must identify that the paper explicitly lists downstream NLP applications of VAD annotations including detecting stance, personality traits, well-being, and cyber-bullying.

Must capture the motivation that VAD annotations are used to draw inferences about people by analyzing how different groups use language to express meaning and emotions, including analysis of text written or spoken by different groups.
Must mention that the paper discusses analyzing VAD judgments themselves across different groups of people as a way to draw inferences about those groups.

decisions: Which prior VAD lexicons and related non-English resources does the paper cite in its related work section on existing VAD lexicons?

requirements.description: Must identify that the cited prior resources are VAD (valence, arousal, dominance) lexicons or affective norms for words, not generic lexical resources.
Must retrieve content specifically from the paper's related work / existing VAD lexicons discussion, not from methodology or results sections.
Must name the 'Affective Norms of English Words (ANEW)' resource and attribute it to Bradley and Lang with the year 1999.
Must name the 'Warriner et al. Norms' resource and attribute it to Warriner et al. with the year 2013.
Must state that the paper mentions only a small number of VAD lexicons in non-English languages and explicitly identify Redondo et al. (2007) as a Spanish rating-scale lexicon.

decisions: Did the system correctly retrieve and reproduce the review rating scale descriptions and associated affiliation text shown on the slide?

requirements.description: Must identify that the slide content is a 6-point review rating scale with discrete levels labeled 6 through 1, each associated with a qualitative descriptor (Transformative, Exciting, Interesting, Uninspiring, Borderline, Poor).
Must retrieve and state the full definition for rating 'e 6 = Transformative', including that it is 'likely to change our field' and is 'for papers worth best paper consideration'.
Must retrieve and state the full definition for rating 'e 3- = Uninspiring', including that the work 'lacks creativity, originality, or insights' and that the reviewer is 'ambivalent about this one'.
Must retrieve and state the full definition for rating 'e 1 = Poor', including the phrase 'I cannot find any reason for this submission to be accepted.'

Must capture and reproduce the affiliation/footer text indicating 'National Research Council Canada' and '@SaifM Mohammad Canada' (or equivalent contiguous text showing institutional name and author handle) as it appears on the slide.

decisions: Does the system correctly identify and describe how traditional Likert item and Likert scale rating methods are characterized in the paper, as reflected in the example slide text?

requirements.description: Must state that the paper discusses traditional rating scale methods (e.g., Likert-type scales) as a baseline or contrast to Best-Worst Scaling for obtaining human ratings of valence, arousal, and dominance.

Must explain that a Likert item is a single statement (e.g., about an interface being user friendly) to which annotators indicate their level of agreement on an ordered response scale (such as strongly agree to strongly disagree).

Must specify that a Likert scale is defined in the paper as the sum or aggregation of responses across multiple Likert items, matching the note that 'a Likert scale is the sum of responses on several Likert items.'

Must describe that the paper (or associated presentation material) includes an illustrative example Likert item with a sentence about a website having a user-friendly interface and a response line showing ordered options from strong agreement to disagreement.

Must cover the part of the paper (or methodological discussion) where traditional rating scale / Likert-type annotation methods are introduced and contrasted with Best-Worst Scaling, including their role in collecting VAD ratings.

decisions: What specific problems with traditional rating scale methods does the paper identify that motivate the use of Best-Worst Scaling for obtaining VAD annotations?

requirements.description: Must identify that the paper explicitly discusses limitations or problems of traditional rating scale methods in the context of collecting valence, arousal, and dominance (VAD) annotations.
Must state that one problem with rating scales described in the paper is that it is difficult for an annotator to be self-consistent across many items.
Must state that another problem with rating scales described in the paper is scale region bias (annotators tending to use only a subset of the available scale).

Must attribute the discussion of rating scale problems to the specific part of the paper where annotation methodology or data collection issues are analyzed (e.g., the section describing annotation procedure or comparison with traditional rating scales).
Must connect the identified rating scale problems (self-consistency difficulty and scale region bias) to the paper's motivation for adopting Best-Worst Scaling as an alternative annotation method.

decisions: How does the paper describe the comparative annotation approach for obtaining human ratings of a property X (e.g., valence) between word pairs, including its cognitive and annotation-cost characteristics?

requirements.description: Must state that the annotation scheme involves presenting two terms (words) at a time and asking which term is more X, where X is the property of interest (e.g., positive, useful).
Must explicitly connect this pairwise comparison setup to the paper's comparative/Best-Worst or similar scaling method used to obtain fine-grained scores for valence, arousal, and dominance.
Must state that this comparative (pairwise) annotation approach reduces or imposes less cognitive load on annotators compared to traditional rating-scale methods.
Must state that the comparative annotation approach helps address or improve annotation consistency issues relative to traditional rating-scale annotations.
Must report that the comparative annotation approach requires a large number of annotations on the order of N^2, where N is the number of terms to be annotated.

decisions: How does the paper describe the Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) annotation procedure used to obtain valence (or other property) ratings for words?

requirements.description: Must state that Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) is the annotation method used to obtain human ratings for the target property (e.g., valence) of words.
Must specify that each BWS annotation task presents the annotator with exactly four items (words), typically denoted as A, B, C, and D.
Must describe that the annotator is asked two questions for each 4-tuple: which word has the most/highest value of the property X and which word has the least/lowest value of X.
Must explain that from the two best-worst choices on a 4-tuple, five out of the six possible pairwise inequalities (comparisons) between the four words' property values are determined.

Must include the specific example that if word A is chosen as highest valence and word D as lowest valence among A, B, C, and D, then the implied ordering constraints between A, B, C, and D are known (i.e., A > B, A > C, A > D, B > D, C > D).

decisions: How does the paper describe using Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) to derive real-valued valence (or other property) scores for words, and what advantages does this method provide?

requirements.description: Must state that each Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) question (choice set) is presented to multiple annotators, as described in the paper's explanation of the BWS annotation procedure.
Must explain that real-valued scores for all terms are obtained using a simple counting method that aggregates how often each term is chosen as 'best' versus 'worst' in the BWS questions.

Must specify that the resulting scores for each term are on a scale ranging from -1 (least X, where X is the property of interest such as valence) to +1 (most X), as defined in the paper's description of the scoring scheme.

Must state that the computed BWS scores can be used to rank all terms along the target property dimension (e.g., valence), as explicitly mentioned in the paper's discussion of how the scores are used.

Must mention that the BWS approach preserves the comparative nature of judgments, requires approximately 2N annotations for N items, and leads to more reliable, less biased, and more discriminating annotations compared to traditional rating scales, as claimed in the paper's methodological motivation section.

decisions: What institutional and author-identification information from the paper must be retrieved to correctly reproduce the title slide header text?

requirements.description: Must identify that the work is associated with the National Research Council Canada (NRC), as indicated in the paper's author/affiliation block.
Must identify that the French name 'Conseil national de recherches Canada' appears as part of the institutional affiliation in the paper.
Must retrieve the author name 'Saif M. Mohammad' from the paper's author list.
Must retrieve the author's Twitter handle or social media identifier '@SaifMMohammad' if it is present in the paper's title/author/footnote metadata.

Must recognize that the bilingual institutional branding (English 'National Research Council Canada' and French 'Conseil national de recherches Canada') is presented together as a header or logo-like element in the paper and should be reproduced together on the slide.

decisions: How did the authors select and compile the set of English terms included in the NRC VAD Lexicon?

requirements.description: Must state that the term selection aimed to include (1) commonly used English terms, (2) terms common in tweets, and (3) terms that denotate or connotate emotions, as explicitly listed in the term selection description.
Must identify that all terms from the NRC Emotion Lexicon (Mohammad and Turney, 2013), approximately 14,000 entries, were included as a source list for term selection.

Must specify that the NRC Emotion Lexicon terms are labeled for association with eight basic emotions: anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and trust, following Plutchik (1980).
Must mention that all terms from the Warriner et al. valence–arousal–dominance lexicon were included as a distinct source in the term selection process.

Must report that high-frequency content terms, including emoticons, from the Hashtag Emotion Corpus (a tweets corpus) (Mohammad, 2012), approximately 1,000 items, were included, and that terms from Roget's Thesaurus categories corresponding to the eight basic emotions were also used as a source.

decisions: How does the paper describe the design of the Best-Worst Scaling questionnaire items and the associated ethics approval for the study?

requirements.description: Must state that the questionnaire uses Best-Worst Scaling questions where participants choose words associated with the LEAST level of a construct (e.g., least happiness/pleasure/positiveness/satisfaction/contentedness/hopefulness OR least unhappiness/annoyance/negativeness/dissatisfaction/melancholy/despair) from a set of four words.
Must specify that each Best-Worst question presents exactly four words as options from which the participant selects the least-associated word.
Must indicate that analogous Best-Worst questions are used not only for valence (happiness/unhappiness) but also for arousal and dominance.

Must reference the part of the paper that describes the questionnaire or annotation procedure (e.g., the section detailing Best-Worst Scaling question wording and structure) rather than unrelated sections such as results or lexicon statistics.

Must report that the study received ethics approval from the NRC Research Ethics Board (NRC-REB) and include the specific protocol number 2017-98, along with the statement that REB review ensures research involving humans meets Canadian standards of ethics.

decisions: How does the paper implement crowdsourcing quality control using internally annotated gold questions and accuracy thresholds?

requirements.description: Must state that approximately 2% of the data was annotated internally by the author and used as gold questions for quality control.
Must explain that the internally annotated gold questions are interspersed among the regular crowdsourcing questions rather than presented in a separate block.
Must describe that when a worker answers a gold question incorrectly, they are immediately notified of the error to provide feedback and improve task understanding.
Must report that if a worker's accuracy on gold questions falls below an 80% threshold, they are refused further annotation and all of their annotations are discarded.
Must explicitly connect the use of gold questions and the 80% accuracy threshold to the goal of preventing malicious or random annotations in the crowdsourced data.

decisions: What information about the NRC VAD Lexicon’s Best-Worst Scaling annotation setup and dataset statistics is needed to generate this slide?

requirements.description: Must state that valence, arousal, and dominance (VAD) scores for words are obtained using Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) rather than traditional rating scales.
Must describe that annotations are collected on 4-tuples of words (items), with multiple annotations per 4-tuple, as specified in the paper’s description of the BWS annotation procedure.
Must retrieve from the relevant table or dataset description the approximate number of annotators per task (around 1000 annotators for each VAD dimension).

Must retrieve from the table summarizing the dataset the columns or statistics for: number of words (#words), number of items (#Items, i.e., 4-tuples), number of annotators (#Annotators), mean annotations per item (MAI), number of questions per item (#Q/Item), and total number of annotations.
Must identify and report the statistic describing the minimum and median number of annotations per 4-tuple, as given in the paper’s annotation statistics section or table.

decisions: What information from the paper is needed to construct a slide showing example word entries and their VAD scores from the NRC VAD Lexicon, including the score range and dimension labeling?

requirements.description: Must state that the lexicon provides human ratings for the three dimensions valence, arousal, and dominance (VAD) for individual English words.
Must retrieve that each word in the NRC VAD Lexicon is associated with a numerical score for each VAD dimension, and that these scores are continuous values rather than categorical labels.

Must specify that the VAD scores in the lexicon are normalized to lie in the range from 0 (lowest valence/arousal/dominance) to 1 (highest valence/arousal/dominance), matching the slide statement about score range.

Must use the section or subsection that presents example entries or a sample of the NRC VAD Lexicon (e.g., a table listing words with their VAD scores) as the primary source for constructing the slide.
Must preserve the tabular structure showing at least two columns pairing 'Word' with its corresponding 'Score' for a given VAD dimension, consistent with the example-entries layout used in the paper.

decisions: How does the paper define and quantify the reliability of annotation consistency using split-half reliability and Pearson correlation?

requirements.description: Must state that 'average split-half reliability (SHR)' is used as a commonly used approach to determine annotation consistency.
